lead.title: Tech billionaires gained USD 845 billion in nine months while every other kind of fortune lost USD 62 billion, Bloomberg's index shows
lead.standfirst: The record divergence means the households a private service professional is most likely to be hired by are increasingly those of the technology founder.
lead.body:
The world's technology billionaires added a combined USD 845 billion to their fortunes in the first nine months of 2026, through 30 September, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. It is a record for the period. Over the same stretch, billionaires whose wealth comes from other industries collectively lost USD 62 billion, as reported by Quartz on 5 October.

The roughly 100 technology fortunes on the index now total USD 4.6 trillion, or 36 per cent of the index's combined wealth. The same week, Bloomberg reported that the artificial intelligence boom had lifted Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg into the top ten of its ranking, a sign of how quickly the head of the list is being redrawn by a single theme.

The concentration matters for anyone who serves wealthy families. Technology wealth tends to be younger, more liquid and more exposed to a single sector than the industrial, retail or property fortunes it is overtaking. It often arrives with households that are being built from scratch: first estates, first aircraft, first full-time staff, and a founder who has never employed a house manager.

It also tends to bring a different set of expectations, from data discipline and digital privacy to a preference for systems and clear reporting over informal arrangements. Families whose fortunes fell, by contrast, are more likely to be reviewing costs, which tends to show up first in hiring pauses and renegotiated vendor contracts.
lead.why: Where the wealth is growing is where new households are being formed, and the professional who understands a founder's world, its tools and its exposure to one sector, is the one who is hired to build it.
lead.src: Quartz, citing the Bloomberg Billionaires Index

articles.title: Fine wine edges up 2.1 per cent in nine months, led by Italy and Champagne, while Bordeaux stays flat
articles.body:
The Liv-ex 100, the benchmark of about 20 of the most traded fine wines, rose 2.1 per cent from January to September 2026 and 4.4 per cent over twelve months. The broader Liv-ex 1000 gained 1.3 per cent for the year to date and 2.2 per cent over twelve months, according to an analysis published by WineNews on 6 October.

Italy was the standout. The Italy 100 index rose 3.5 per cent year to date and 4.9 per cent over twelve months, the best of any regional index over the past year, and Italian labels hold four of the top ten places in the Liv-ex 100. Champagne 50 gained 4.1 per cent this year, Burgundy 150 rose 1.7 per cent and Rhône 100 rose 0.5 per cent. Bordeaux 500 fell 0.2 per cent and is the only index still negative for the year.

The best individual performers were Bruno Giacosa Barolo Falletto Vigna Le Rocche Riserva 2016, up 31.7 per cent, Giacomo Conterno Barolo Monfortino Riserva 2019, up 19.4 per cent, Soldera Case Basse 2020, up 18.7 per cent, and Antinori Solaia 2021, up 14.1 per cent. The analysis describes the wider wine market as still in a slump, which makes the gains a bright spot concentrated in a small niche of prestige bottles.

For a cellar, the picture is one of rotation rather than a rising tide. Collectors who built their holdings around Bordeaux are seeing little movement, while demand has moved towards the Langhe, Tuscany and grower Champagne.
articles.why: A house manager who looks after a cellar is expected to speak about what is moving and why, and to advise on what to drink, hold or insure, not only on where it is stored.

articles.title: Large-cabin jet sales fell about 25 per cent in the third quarter, yet six months of supply keeps the segment the tightest in the market
articles.body:
Sales of pre-owned large-cabin business jets fell roughly 25 per cent year on year in the third quarter of 2026, and the segment accounted for more than two thirds of the quarter's overall shortfall, according to GlobalAir.com's BrokerBeat report with data to 1 October. Sales for the twelve months to September were still 11 per cent ahead of the prior year, and September itself recovered to roughly the level of September 2025.

Supply has not eased. There were 178 active large-cabin listings, the most of any jet class, representing 6.0 months of supply, the shortest of any turbine segment. The median time on the market was 77 days, the fastest among jets. Large-cabin aircraft made up 37 per cent of the 107 Aircraft Wanted requests sent through BrokerNet in the quarter, the largest share of any class.

Dealers describe a market of selective buyers. One said demand for premium late-model aircraft remains strong, with some receiving offers above asking price. Another expects less of a year-end rush than last year, citing labour shortages, parts delays and limited availability of pre-purchase inspection slots. The October to December 2025 period was the strongest in two years of data, so this quarter faces a hard comparison. IADA-accredited dealers closed 746 deals in the first half, up 21 per cent.

On the delivery side, dealers expect new aircraft from manufacturers to ease supply, with some softening likely in early 2027.
articles.why: A family that owns or charters a large-cabin aircraft depends on its coordinator to understand when an aircraft can be inspected, repositioned or replaced, and a tight maintenance calendar is now part of that planning.

articles.title: UBS counts nearly one million new dollar millionaires as personal wealth grows by more than 10 per cent
articles.body:
The UBS Global Wealth Report 2026, the seventeenth edition, finds that personal wealth rose by more than 10 per cent, its fastest pace in several years. The number of US dollar millionaires grew again, adding nearly one million people worldwide, or more than 2,600 a day.

The report covers 56 markets that UBS says account for more than 92 per cent of the world's wealth, and it examines how the global wealth pyramid is shifting as faster-growing tiers reshape the picture of where affluence is emerging. The firm frames the analysis around how wealth is created, as well as how it is distributed across regions.

For the households at the very top, the relevant point is not the headcount of millionaires but the pace at which new wealth is being created and where. New fortunes mean new houses, new offices and new demand for people who can run them, and they tend to appear in markets where the private service profession is still young and agencies are few.
articles.why: The report is a map of where demand for private staff will come from next, and it rewards candidates who can read wealth data the way their employers do.

briefs.t: Three new yachts from 40 to 80 metres reach the water in a month
briefs.b: Custom Line launched its 40-metre Saetta 128 at Ancona on 8 October, while CRN delivered the 70-metre Cerulean on 16 September and ISA Yachts launched the 80-metre Belita on 15 September. Gulf Craft launched the 30-metre Nomad 101 Charisma on 12 October.
Embraer delivered the first Praetor 600E to Flexjet, the fleet launch customer, on 2 October. Flexjet is also due to receive its first Praetor 500E in the fourth quarter of 2026.

briefs.t: Autoland reaches more private cabins, and Northolt gains an FBO
briefs.b: Pilatus received EASA and FAA approval for Safety Autoland on the PC-12 PRO on 8 October, and Epic won FAA certification for Garmin Autoland on the E1000 AX on 12 October. Gama Aviation began FBO operations at RAF Northolt in West London on 2 October.

lead.title: A family office with USD 1 billion or more now costs USD 6.6 million a year to run, and talent is the reason, J.P. Morgan finds
lead.standfirst: The bank's 2026 survey of 333 single-family offices shows costs climbing as families replace relatives with paid professionals.
lead.body:
The 2026 Global Family Office Report from J.P. Morgan Private Bank draws on 333 single-family offices in more than 30 countries, a sample 75 per cent larger than in 2024. Respondents have an average net worth of about USD 1.6 billion, and 59 per cent are based in the United States. It is one of the most detailed public pictures of what it costs to run the machinery that sits behind a great fortune.

For offices managing USD 1 billion or more, the average annual operating cost is USD 6.6 million, up from USD 6.1 million in the previous report. The scale is steep: about USD 0.9 million a year below USD 250 million, USD 1.7 million between USD 250 million and USD 500 million, and USD 3.3 million between USD 501 million and USD 999 million. The authors name talent as a major driver. Younger offices are often led by family members paid well below market rates, and costs rise as non-family professionals arrive. Investment teams are the most expensive, because they are paid at hedge fund and large asset manager levels.

Outsourcing is the other half of the picture. On average about 26 per cent of costs go to external providers, and more than four in ten offices spend at least 30 per cent externally. Legal work (about 52 per cent) and trading and execution (over 45 per cent) are the functions most often sent outside, along with cybersecurity. Compensation and staffing, financial administration and reporting tend to stay in house.

The pattern describes a profession in transition. As a family office moves from relatives to employees, it needs people who can run payroll, contracts, vendors and confidentiality as carefully as it runs a portfolio, and those functions are the ones families choose to keep close.
lead.why: Staffing and compensation are among the functions families keep in house, which is where a household or estate manager who understands contracts, vendors and discretion becomes part of the office rather than an adjunct to it.
lead.src: J.P. Morgan Private Bank, 2026 Global Family Office Report

articles.title: One in three family offices names over-reliance on a single person or provider as a continuity risk
articles.body:
Alongside its cost findings, the J.P. Morgan report asks family offices what could break their continuity. The external risks are familiar: financial market disruption (46 per cent) and regulatory and tax complexity (38 per cent). The internal list is more revealing. Family conflict or misaligned values, lack of succession planning, and over-reliance on one person or provider each draw 33 per cent.

The last of those is a staffing question as much as a governance one. An office that depends on a single trusted manager, a single assistant or a single outside firm is exposed the day that person leaves, falls ill or is simply approached by someone else. Families respond by documenting procedures, sharing knowledge across a small team and naming deputies.

Governance differs sharply among families that still own an operating company. About 6 in 10 respondents run a business alongside the office. Among them, 41 per cent rank internal conflict among their top three risks, and 20 per cent rank it first, about twice the rate of other families. Sixty-six per cent of business-owning families have a formal constitution or written bylaws, against about 50 per cent of the rest. The report recommends investment committees with outside advisers and fiduciary boards that may include non-family members.
articles.why: A house or estate manager who documents routines, trains a deputy and keeps clear records reduces exactly the single-person dependency that families now list as a risk.
articles.src: J.P. Morgan Private Bank, 2026 Global Family Office Report

articles.title: United States charter demand has risen 27 per cent in a year, Avinode reports, while departures stay stable
articles.body:
Avinode, the marketplace through which operators and brokers trade charter flights, reports that United States charter demand climbed 27 per cent over the past year, according to Aviation International News on 15 October. The subheadline adds that departures have remained stable despite an influx of United States based brokers.

The gap between the two measures is worth reading carefully. Demand measured in requests can grow faster than flights actually flown, particularly when more intermediaries are sending enquiries to the same pool of aircraft. For a principal's team, that can mean more quotes for the same trip, and more need to judge which quote is real.

Technology is entering the same space. FlyJets has taken its JetGPT charter agent out of an eight-month beta, with booking, listing and route alerts, AIN reported on 12 October. The detail of the tool was not available at the time of writing, but the direction is plain: first contact with a charter market is becoming automated.
articles.why: Whoever arranges a family's flights will increasingly compare automated quotes from many brokers, so judgement about operator quality, safety and true availability matters more than speed of response.

articles.title: Art Basel Paris opens its fifth edition under a new director, with 206 galleries and a record 12 joint booths
articles.body:
Art Basel Paris returns to the Grand Palais with preview days on 21 and 22 October and public days from 23 to 25 October. It is the first edition under director Karim Crippa. More than 200 exhibitors from 41 countries and territories take part, with more than 180 in the main Galeries sector, up from 177 last year, and a record 12 joint booths.

Nearly 30 galleries are new to the fair, among them ChertLüdde and Kraupa-Tuskany Zeidler from Berlin, Empty Gallery from Hong Kong, Luxembourg + Co. from London and Pace Di Donna Schrader from New York. More than 60 exhibitors operate spaces in France. Returning names include Gagosian, Hauser & Wirth, David Zwirner, White Cube, Thaddaeus Ropac, Perrotin and Pace. An invitation-only Avant-Première is scheduled for 20 October.

The backdrop is a French market that the Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report 2026 puts at USD 4.5 billion of sales in 2025, up 9 per cent on the year.
articles.why: Fair week means collectors, advisers and their staff converge on one city, and the person arranging the family's access, transport, security and shipping needs to know the calendar, and which days are invitation-only.
articles.src: USA Art News, citing Art Basel

briefs.t: Two thirds of family offices now plan for AI
briefs.b: J.P. Morgan finds that 65 per cent of surveyed single-family offices plan to prioritise AI investments, now or later. Some 43 per cent hold venture or growth equity, averaging 3.3 per cent of their portfolios.

briefs.t: Geopolitics tops the family office risk list
briefs.b: Geopolitics is the leading macro concern for 64 per cent of surveyed offices, ahead of interest rates (61 per cent) and growth (59 per cent). Only 28 per cent hold gold, at an average 0.9 per cent of assets.

briefs.t: Ocorian's family office report covers 25 jurisdictions
briefs.b: Published on 10 April 2026 in six parts, it examines governance, risk, data and AI, and the role of specialist providers to families.

lead.title: Ultra-wealthy donors gave USD 250 billion in 2025, about 38 per cent of all individual giving, and at least 17 per cent of them run a private foundation, Altrata finds
lead.standfirst: Altrata's High Net Worth Philanthropy 2026, published on 15 October, shows giving by the ultra-wealthy outpacing every other source and becoming more structured, more strategic and more global.
lead.body:
Altrata's eighth High Net Worth Philanthropy report, released on 15 October, puts giving by ultra high net worth individuals (those with USD 30 million or more) at USD 250 billion in 2025. That is about 38 per cent of everything given by individuals worldwide, a pool that topped USD 650 billion. UHNW giving is up 32 per cent on 2022 levels and has grown 7.3 per cent a year from 2018 to 2025, faster than giving by other individuals or by foundations.

The donors are a small group. Altrata counts about 557,000 UHNW individuals, a little over half a million people, inside a wider population of 5.8 million people worth USD 5 million or more, forecast to reach 8.3 million by 2031. Their liquid assets stood at USD 33 trillion in 2025 and are expected to pass USD 45 trillion by 2031. North America accounts for USD 115 billion of the UHNW total, or 46 per cent. Europe is up 35 per cent since 2022 and Asia up 42 per cent, the second-fastest rise of any region. New York, Seoul and Hong Kong lead Altrata's Giving Opportunity Index of 100 cities.

The report also describes how the money moves. At least 17 per cent of UHNW individuals hold a private foundation, and Altrata notes a shift towards transformational impact, closer due diligence and succession planning. Education is the most common cause, with about 60 per cent of wealthy donors giving to it at least once in the past decade. Environmental giving took a 26 per cent higher share in 2021 to 2025 than in 2015 to 2020, and healthcare and medical research gained 15 per cent in relative share. With public funding and multilateral aid declining in many countries, the report expects reliance on individual and corporate giving to grow, although it says private philanthropy cannot fully replace institutional aid.

The generational picture matters as much as the totals. Gen Z and Millennials make up 6 per cent of the wealthy today and are projected to reach 37 per cent by 2040. Women's share of the UHNW population is forecast to rise from 12 per cent to 19 per cent over the same period, and among wealthy donors women's median number of gifts over the past decade was 1.7 times that of men. The donor base, Altrata concludes, is becoming younger, more global and more digitally oriented.
lead.why: In many principal households giving is run from the house or the family office, through foundation calendars, gala seasons, site visits and due diligence. Anyone who manages that diary needs to understand the structures behind it, and to handle the discretion that surrounds who gives, to what and when.

articles.title: Confidentiality can add 15 to 20 per cent to a household salary, and 77 per cent of Los Angeles assistant roles now require an NDA, Morgan & Mallet's research shows
articles.body:
Morgan & Mallet's Beyond the Butler 2025/26 report, as summarised by Spear's, describes a household staffing market in which demand is rising while qualified supply shrinks. The agency's central finding is that discretion has become a priced skill. Confidentiality requirements can raise pay by 15 to 20 per cent, and in Los Angeles 77 per cent of personal assistant roles carry a non-disclosure agreement.

The technical bar is rising alongside it. In San Francisco, 83 per cent of recent positions required smart-home integration, and the report estimates that new staff typically need eight to twelve weeks to adapt to a household's systems. Estate managers are the hardest hire of all: they account for 10 per cent of US requests, yet few candidates combine the technical, security and management experience the role demands. Average tenure across the market is about three years, although in Los Angeles 92 per cent of the personal assistants the agency has placed stay beyond two years.

Geography is pulling the market in several directions. The United States offers the highest pay in 60 per cent of household roles, with private chefs earning up to USD 300,000 and executive assistants up to USD 250,000, and estate managers and chiefs of staff in a similar range. UAE compensation is expected to reach USD 120,000 to USD 140,000. In the United Kingdom, limited access to EU workers keeps London pay rising, while the end of the non-dom regime has sent many families to Florida, Dubai and Switzerland, and each new home needs staff who can work across borders.

Family structures vary by country as well. Nannies make up nearly a quarter of UK placements, and worldwide nanny placements have a 96 per cent success rate, with candidates usually bringing about six years of experience. In France, domestic couples account for 21 per cent of the most senior staffing requests.
articles.why: Discretion, systems fluency and the ability to move between homes are now what the market pays for. A candidate who can show all three, with evidence, sits in the narrowest part of the supply curve.

articles.title: A de Kooning set a European record at Sotheby's London, yet the Contemporary Evening Sale fell short of its low estimate
articles.body:
Sotheby's London Contemporary Evening Sale on Thursday 15 October made GBP 36.9 million at hammer, below the GBP 39.5 million low estimate, and GBP 45.9 million with fees, slightly under last October's GBP 47.6 million. Of 34 lots offered after three were withdrawn, six went unsold, a sell-through rate of 82 per cent. Only about 30 per cent of lots hammered above their low estimate, according to The Art Newspaper.

The top lot was Willem de Kooning's Untitled (1977), a guaranteed work that opened at GBP 7 million, below its GBP 8 million low estimate, and hammered at GBP 8.2 million, or GBP 9.8 million with fees. That is a European auction record for the artist and two and a half times its 2015 price in New York. Gerhard Richter's Abstraktes Bild (1992) made GBP 6.7 million with fees, slightly below its low estimate. A David Hockney iPad drawing made GBP 1.9 million with fees, three times its low estimate and a record for an iPad work by the artist, and a Michael Andrews work on paper made GBP 704,000, nearly five times its high estimate.

The weak spots were at the young end of the market. A 2021 Yayoi Kusama sculpture hammered at GBP 250,000, a quarter of its GBP 1 million low estimate, and works by Lynette Yiadom-Boakye and Jadé Fadojutimi went unsold. Dealer Thomas Stauffer, quoted in the report, said collectors are cautious and set limits conservatively low, and he called the unsold ultra-contemporary lots concerning. The same mood was noted at Frieze London.

The backdrop is still strong. Sotheby's London has now passed USD 1 billion of total sales in 2026, and its modern and contemporary sales have reached GBP 598 million, the highest year-to-date figure since 2015.
articles.why: Collectors who buy with discipline are the ones a house manager meets: guarantees, reserves and estimates shape what is bought and when. Understanding why a record can coexist with a muted sale lets you brief a principal's advisers, and handle a viewing or a transport schedule, with credibility.

articles.title: A steel Voutilainen made USD 1.02 million against an estimate of USD 120,000 to USD 240,000 as October's watch sales rewarded rarity over name
articles.body:
Early October's watch auctions, tallied by Haute Time, point in one direction: the steepest multiples went to pieces that are hard to replace. At Phillips New York's online Sessions sale, which closed on 9 October with all 88 lots sold, a Voutilainen 28Sport in steel, number 5 of 8, made USD 1,016,000 with premium. Two F.P. Journe watches made USD 304,800 each, and a Jaeger-LeCoultre Atmos Gustav Klimt clock passed its high estimate at USD 152,400.

At Sotheby's Paris on 7 October, a fresh-to-market Rolex Daytona Paul Newman Reference 6241 from about 1968 made EUR 448,000 against an estimate of EUR 120,000 to EUR 260,000, after 15 bids. Christie's Hong Kong online sale closed at HKD 23.1 million, with an Eska pink gold enamel-dial wristwatch reaching HKD 1.2 million against an estimate of HKD 80,000 to HKD 160,000. Bonhams New York on 8 October was led by an Audemars Piguet Royal Oak at USD 76,700.

The softer side was the modern, large-estimate end. Haute Time notes that high-value modern Patek Philippe watches in Hong Kong sold within their ranges on few bids, and a Moser tourbillon and a Streamliner did not sell at Bonhams.

The next test is Geneva. Christie's online Geneva Edit runs from 15 to 22 October, Phillips holds The Geneva Watch Auction XXIV on 7 and 8 November with 221 lots, and Sotheby's and Christie's hold their live sales on 8 and 9 November.
articles.why: Watches are part of the language of the households you will serve, as gifts, heirlooms and working tools of a principal. Knowing why one piece out-sells a famous name lets you handle insurance, travel and custody of a collection with the right level of care.

briefs.b: Altrata's World Ultra Wealth Report 2026 counts 556,850 people worth USD 30 million or more, up 14.4 per cent and the fastest annual rise since 2017, holding USD 63.8 trillion between them. New York has almost 24,000 and Seoul 6,220, up by more than a third. Altrata forecasts 746,570 by 2030.

briefs.t: Geneva's autumn watch week is set for 7 to 9 November
briefs.b: Phillips sells 221 lots at the Hotel President Wilson on 7 and 8 November, led by a 1945 Patek Philippe Reference 1436 estimated at CHF 2 million to CHF 4 million. Christie's holds its live sale on 9 November, including 21 charity watches for ELA.

briefs.t: Rota and live-in terms shape what a household really pays
briefs.b: Cora Partners' September guide notes that live-in roles carry a lower base salary because housing and utilities are covered, while two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off rota posts command a premium and are standard for security and some senior management. Travelling chefs, butlers and nannies sit at the top of their bands.

lead.title: Prime home prices rose 2.6 per cent worldwide in the year to June, but Tokyo climbed 50.7 per cent, Knight Frank's index shows
lead.standfirst: The latest Prime Global Cities Index finds growth picking up slightly overall, with Asian cities doing nearly all the work.
lead.body:
Knight Frank's Prime Global Cities Index, which tracks prime residential markets in 47 cities, recorded a 2.6 per cent rise in prime prices in the 12 months to the second quarter of 2026. That is up from 2 per cent in the previous quarter, though still below the 3 per cent growth recorded a year earlier. The headline is modest. The spread underneath it is not.

Tokyo led the table with annual growth of 50.7 per cent, the highest in the index. Manila followed at 14.6 per cent, Singapore at 9.5 per cent, Seoul at 6.4 per cent and Mumbai at 6.2 per cent, with Bengaluru at 4.5 per cent. Mumbai's prime prices rose 1.7 per cent in the second quarter alone. The cities that dominate the private service conversation, London, New York and Geneva, do not feature among the leaders.

For a principal, a prime address is rarely a single decision. It is a second, third or fourth residence added to a portfolio that already includes a main house, a country estate and often a yacht berth. When values in one city jump by half in a year, the household may revisit where it holds property, which of its homes are staffed full time, and where it would rather be present for part of the year.

That has practical consequences for the people who run these homes. A new residence in Tokyo or Singapore needs a house manager, a security plan, local employment contracts and suppliers who understand the family's standards. A property that sits empty for ten months needs a different kind of caretaker arrangement. The index measures prices, but each shift it records eventually lands on a manager's desk as a staffing and logistics question.
lead.why: Where a family buys, it eventually staffs, so a price index is also an early signal of where private service roles will open.

articles.title: Superyacht brokerage sales reached EUR 4.05 billion in the first half, and a 100-metre Feadship went for a quarter of it in under six months
articles.body: Sales of yachts of 24 metres and over totalled EUR 4.05 billion between January and June 2026, according to BoatPro, the market-intelligence platform of Boat International. A total of 281 yachts changed hands, 129 in the first quarter and 152 in the second. A year earlier the figure was 272 yachts and EUR 3.61 billion, and in the first half of 2024 it was 225 yachts and EUR 2.21 billion. The average asking value of yachts sold rose to EUR 14.4 million, from EUR 13.28 million in 2025 and EUR 9.83 million in 2024. The largest deal was Moonrise, the 100.7-metre Feadship, sold by Burgess in just under six months at an asking price of EUR 325 million. Other large sales included the 89-metre Amels Mirage, formerly Here Comes the Sun, with an estimated asking value of EUR 165 million, the 66.3-metre Hampshire at EUR 85 million and the 61-metre Jubilee at EUR 73.5 million. BoatPro notes that values reflect each yacht's last-known asking price, because final prices are generally confidential. The mid-size band moved most. Sales of yachts from 50 to 70 metres rose 52.9 per cent, from 17 to 26 transactions, and those from 40 to 50 metres rose 10 per cent, while the 30 to 40 metre band fell 6 per cent. Smaller yachts still produced the most transactions overall, and limited availability may have held back some results. Every sale of this kind sets a handover in motion. A yacht changing owners often means a new captain and crew, a survey, a refit schedule, a flag and tax review and a rewritten operating budget. For the shore-side manager, who coordinates with the yacht's captain on behalf of the principal, a change of ownership is a period of intense administration.
articles.why: A busy brokerage market means frequent ownership changes, and each one hands the principal's shore-side team a long list of transitions to coordinate.

articles.title: Art Basel Paris opens to preview guests on 21 October with more than 200 galleries, as Christie's reports its strongest first half in five years
articles.body: Art Basel Paris returns to the Grand Palais for its fifth edition, with preview days on 21 and 22 October, a public vernissage on the evening of 22 October and public days from 23 to 25 October. More than 200 galleries from over 40 countries are taking part, under Karim Crippa, who leads his first edition as director. The main Galeries sector brings more than 180 Modern, postwar and contemporary dealers, including nearly 30 first-time participants. Emergence offers 16 solo booths, Premise has nine curatorial projects, and a record 12 joint booth presentations are on the plan. The fair arrives after a strong spring and summer for the auction houses. Christie's reported first-half sales of USD 4.5 billion, up 71 per cent from a year earlier and described as its best midyear in five years. Auction sales made USD 3.5 billion at a 91 per cent sell-through rate, and private sales added USD 1 billion. Twentieth and twenty-first century art accounted for USD 2.3 billion, led by Jackson Pollock's Number 7A at USD 181.2 million. The luxury category reached USD 539 million, up 15 per cent, helped by a boom in watches. Paris will be busy beyond the fair itself, with exhibitions at the Musée d'Orsay, the Musée Picasso and the Fondation Louis Vuitton. For collectors, the week combines viewing appointments, dinners, private previews and gallery visits, usually in a tight sequence. A household that collects will often ask its manager or concierge to arrange the practical side of the week: access to preview days, transport that can cross a closed-off central Paris, hotel or residence logistics, shipping and condition reporting for anything bought, and a discreet schedule for the principal's advisers.
articles.why: A principal who collects expects the team to know the fair calendar and its logistics, and to protect the principal's time during a very crowded week.

articles.title: Business jet activity rose 5.6 per cent in July worldwide, but Europe slipped and large cabin flying there fell 6.5 per cent, ARGUS data shows
articles.body:
ARGUS reported that global business jet activity in July 2026 was up 5.6 per cent year on year and 4.4 per cent on June. North America grew 4.3 per cent, led by fractional operators at 10 per cent, followed by charter at 4.8 per cent and owner-operated flying at 1.4 per cent. Every aircraft category increased.

Europe told a different story. Activity fell 1.2 per cent year on year, its first decline since April 2025, although it rose 4.3 per cent from June. Midsize cabin flights were up 1.8 per cent and turboprops up 3 per cent, but small cabin fell 0.9 per cent and large cabin fell 6.5 per cent. Africa, Asia, Australia and South America combined rose 18.5 per cent, with turboprops up 23.9 per cent.

WingX, which tracks weekly data, found that activity in the week of 27 July to 2 August was down 2.4 per cent, the third consecutive weekly decline and the first such run since late 2024. Even so, year-to-date activity was up 3.2 per cent, and charter departures had grown 10.2 per cent. Owner-operated flying, the largest segment at about 1.1 million departures, grew just 0.6 per cent. The report framed the second half as a test of whether the dips were seasonal or the start of a normalisation.

The pattern matters because families increasingly mix ownership, fractional shares and charter. A concierge who books flights has to understand which of those options is available at short notice on a given route.
articles.why: Charter and fractional growth means more families rely on booking skill rather than a dedicated aircraft, which puts the concierge's knowledge of operators at a premium.

briefs.t: Sixty per cent of family offices plan to change their asset allocation
briefs.b: UBS's Global Family Office Report 2026, based on 307 family offices with an average net worth of USD 2.7 billion, found that 60 per cent intend to adjust strategic allocation in the next 12 months, a first for the study. Some 65 per cent have invested across the AI value chain, and about one third have a clearly defined succession plan.

briefs.t: Estate manager salaries span USD 120,000 to more than USD 300,000
briefs.b: A payroll provider's 2026 guide puts US estate manager base pay at USD 120,000 to USD 300,000 or more, house managers at USD 80,000 to USD 200,000 or more and personal chefs at USD 90,000 to USD 300,000 or more. Employers also owe 7.65 per cent in Social Security and Medicare tax on gross pay, plus unemployment and insurance costs.

briefs.t: The Monaco Yacht Show fleet was younger and mostly for sale
briefs.b: The September show listed 117 superyachts with an average age of 6.47 years, down from 7.28 a year earlier, and 79 world or show debuts. Seventy yachts were for sale, with combined asking prices of about USD 2.5 billion.

lead.title: Sixty-two per cent of family offices give household staff no security training, and only 4 per cent call what they offer sufficient
lead.standfirst: A new survey of family office security finds that the people closest to a principal are the least prepared, even as targeting of wealthy families rises.
lead.body:
The State of Family Office Security 2026, a 103-page study by Presage Global and Nines, reports that 62 per cent of family offices provide no formal security training to household staff. Only 4 per cent say the training they do provide is sufficient. The findings were reported by Family Wealth Report on 24 June 2026.

The gap matters because of how threats now arrive. AI-powered attacks are the top emerging concern for 65 per cent of respondents, and a convincing voice, email or message aimed at a driver, a housekeeper or an assistant is often cheaper to attempt than a breach of the principal's own systems. Yet only 7 per cent of respondents provide formal cybersecurity training to family members, so the weakness is not confined to the staff room.

The survey also shows how reactive most households remain. Some 47 per cent of family offices have never conducted a risk assessment, or conduct one only after an incident. Sixty per cent of security improvements follow an incident, against 19 per cent triggered by regular assessments, and the group that acts only reactively reported the highest incident rate, at 45 per cent.

The commercial signs point the same way. Dale Buckner, chief executive of Global Guardian, told Family Wealth Report that the firm's revenues rose 47 per cent year on year in 2025 and its executive protection work grew 71 per cent. He said targeting of high-net-worth individuals has increased even as overall crime in the United States has fallen, with organised groups using sophisticated methods.
lead.why: For an estate manager, security awareness is becoming part of the job description: someone who can brief a household on verification calls, visitor protocols and device hygiene is more valuable than the survey suggests most families have.

articles.title: Henley drops its millionaire headcount and ranks countries on how well they compete for mobile wealth
articles.body:
Henley & Partners published its Private Wealth Migration Report 2026 in June with a changed method. According to analysis from The Family Office Almanac, it no longer gives a precise count of millionaires moving between countries, saying the data does not yet support one, and its single named author has been removed. The headline is now a Wealth Mobility Competitiveness Score out of 100.

The change follows years of criticism. Dan Neidle of Tax Policy Associates and the Tax Justice Network had questioned the reliability of the earlier headcounts, particularly the figures on the United Kingdom. The new report instead says applications to Henley's own migration services from people with a UK address rose about 15 per cent over 2024 and 2025, a different measure from the earlier outflow claims.

On the scores, as reported by Wealth Professional, the United Arab Emirates leads at 85.3 and has been the top destination for relocating millionaires for two years. Singapore scores 79.5, New Zealand 75.8, the Cayman Islands 74.3 and Cyprus 73.5. The United Kingdom scores 68.3 and France 65.7, while the United States scores 62.3. The report describes a paradox in which the United States is both the largest private wealth market and the largest source of applications for residence or citizenship elsewhere.

Henley's central message is multijurisdictional living: wealthy families spreading residence, citizenship and business interests across several countries rather than anchoring to one. Enquiries from UAE-based individuals rose 41 per cent between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, as residents prepared contingency options amid regional conflict.
articles.why: A family holding several residences and passports needs a household that can open, close and move between them; understanding why principals diversify helps whoever runs the logistics.
articles.src: The Family Office Almanac / Wealth Professional

articles.title: Hong Kong's autumn auctions pass HK$2 billion as younger buyers arrive
articles.body:
Sotheby's, Christie's and Phillips held their autumn marquee sales in Hong Kong from 28 to 30 September, and the South China Morning Post reported on 1 October that they together topped HK$2 billion, about USD 255.8 million. The spring series had totalled HK$1.3 billion.

Christie's took HK$956.5 million, up 17 per cent on the year. Sotheby's took HK$956 million, up 35 per cent on its March series, with a 91 per cent sell-through rate and five artist records. Christie's also reported a 30 per cent rise in new young buyers and broad international participation.

The newspaper linked the results to steady demand for leading Western and Asian art and to competitive bidding for works fresh to the market with strong provenance. Works by Yayoi Kusama, however, received what the headline called a cool reception, a reminder that even a rising market is selective.

The lead image of the report was Leonard Tsuguharu Foujita's Chatte et chaton of 1932, sold at Sotheby's on 28 September.
articles.why: Collections are managed as living assets, and a manager who knows which markets are firming and which names are cooling can speak credibly to advisers, registrars and the family.

articles.title: Lürssen delivered six yachts totalling 655 metres in 105 days this spring
articles.body:
Superyachts.com reported on 29 July that the German builder Lürssen delivered six yachts between March and June 2026, in 105 days, with a combined length of 655 metres. Five of the six exceed 100 metres, and the yard says it has built more than 30 yachts above that length.

The largest was Deep Blue at 134.2 metres, about which few official details have been released. Boardwalk measures 117 metres and Nausicaä 114.2 metres, the latter with exterior design by Marc Newson. O3, at 109 metres, was built for long-range exploration including Greenland and Antarctica. Nixie, at 102.4 metres, made her public debut at the Monaco Yacht Show and carries a six-metre glass pool, while Odisea, at 78.2 metres, favours a beach club over a traditional saloon.

The article names no owners and gives no crew numbers. Peter Lürssen called delivering six yachts in one year a remarkable achievement.
articles.why: Every delivery of this size brings a new crew, a new household afloat and new demands on shore teams, from provisioning to port agents and guest transfers.

briefs.t: Italy's flat tax stays in view as the UAE wobbles
briefs.b: Henley data cited by EnterpriseAM showed enquiries for Italy's residence programme up 5 per cent between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first of 2026. The regime lets foreign residents pay a flat EUR 300,000 a year on overseas income.

briefs.t: Gulf residents build a second option
briefs.b: Henley says applications for alternative residence or citizenship from UAE-based individuals rose 29 per cent between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first of 2026. It describes the shift as optionality rather than departure.

briefs.t: Executive protection is the fastest growing line
briefs.b: Global Guardian reports its executive protection work grew 71 per cent in 2025, ahead of 47 per cent growth in total revenues. Its chief executive attributes the rise to organised groups targeting wealthy individuals.

lead.title: Technology billionaires account for all of the USD 845 billion of new wealth made in 2026, Bloomberg finds, while fortunes built elsewhere are USD 62 billion poorer
lead.standfirst: Elon Musk now stands at USD 977 billion and Michael Dell has added USD 89.1 billion, in a ranking where the whole of the year's gain sits in a single industry.
lead.body:
Bloomberg's Billionaires Index, as reported on 5 October, shows that billionaires with technology fortunes account for the entire USD 845 billion of wealth gained so far this year. Billionaires whose fortunes sit outside technology are, taken together, USD 62 billion poorer over the same period. The year's gains have not been shared across the list. They have been collected by one sector.

At the top, Elon Musk is shown at USD 977 billion. Michael Dell added USD 89.1 billion to reach USD 229 billion, the second-largest dollar gain on the index after Mr Musk's. Bloomberg also flags signs that the surge may be nearing its peak, a caution worth holding beside the headline numbers. These are estimates of paper wealth that move with share prices every day, not cash in an account.

For the private service market, the significance lies in how the wealth is held. A fortune concentrated in the shares of one company is a different household from a diversified one. Its net worth can move by billions in a week, and liquidity tends to arrive in events, such as a sale of stock, a listing or a vesting date, rather than as a steady income. Decisions about houses, aircraft and staff can follow those events rather than the calendar.

Those who serve such families tend to see the effect in the diary before they see it in the headline. Purchases and hires can cluster around liquidity, and a principal whose wealth is tied to one company may also carry a public profile tied to that company, with the privacy and security questions that follow. The index is a measure of wealth. What it implies for a household is something the person running that household has to read for herself.
lead.why: A household's spending rhythm follows how its wealth is held, so a manager who understands concentration, liquidity events and public exposure can plan staffing, security and cash far better than one who reads only the headline net worth.
lead.src: Bloomberg Billionaires Index, via AI Weekly

articles.title: Jet card prices fell 3.1 per cent in the third quarter, the lowest reading since late 2023, even as the two largest business jet makers carry order books worth close to USD 46 billion
articles.body:
Private Jet Card Comparisons reported on 5 October that jet card rates fell 3.1 per cent in the third quarter, the lowest reading since the fourth quarter of 2023. Aviation International News, summarising the same data, reports rates down both from the previous quarter and from a year earlier, with the turboprop category leading the declines after the pause at OneFlight. In July the same index had shown rates up about half a point on the year but down about one point since the first quarter, so the softening has been building through 2026.

The pricing sits oddly beside the manufacturers' books. Forecast International's analysis of 7 August puts Bombardier's backlog at USD 21.8 billion at the end of the second quarter, up from USD 17.5 billion at the end of 2025, and Gulfstream's at USD 24.0 billion, up from USD 21.8 billion. Bombardier delivered 56 aircraft in the first half and guides to more than 157 for the year, while Gulfstream delivered 79 and guides to roughly 160. Both booked more than they delivered in the second quarter, with a book-to-bill ratio of 1.5 times at each.

The two trends are not contradictory. A jet card is a prepaid block of hours on someone else's fleet, so its price reflects charter supply, demand and the health of operators. A backlog reflects owners who want their own aircraft and will wait for it, and Forecast notes build cycles of 12 to 24 months at Bombardier. The likeliest reading is that a softer card market is a good moment to buy hours, while a full backlog shows that for some principals ownership remains the aim.

For whoever organises a family's flying, a cheaper quarter is an opening to compare and renegotiate, not a reason to read the contract less closely. The sharpest fall came in the category that followed a provider's pause, and a card is only as good as the operator standing behind it.
articles.why: Card pricing, operator health and aircraft waiting times are three separate dials, and the person who arranges a family's flying is the one expected to know which of them has moved before the next renewal.
articles.src: Aviation International News, Private Jet Card Comparisons, Forecast International

articles.title: A Beaune domaine reports red yields 50 to 70 per cent below normal on the first day of the 2026 harvest, and the cellar a house is buying for will hold fewer bottles
articles.body:
Bill Nanson's Burgundy Report diary for 24 August, the first day of picking at a domaine in Beaune, records yields well down. Reds are usually 50 to 70 per cent below normal and whites often down by as much as half. Bunches are consistently small, and there is, in his words, very little juice in them.

The cause given is water stress. Well-draining slope parcels suffered most, with many yellowing leaves, and even the lower alluvial parcels drained too freely this year. On quality, the early signs are kind: sorting needed little work, and the pinot noir was ripe but pure, with no prune or overdone notes at this stage. The domaine's head played down the difference between 13 and 15 hectolitres per hectare, provided the fruit has been well sorted. Thunder and heavy rain arrived that evening.

The caution is plain. This is one domaine on one day, and the report does not describe the vintage as a whole. Other growers and other appellations may have fared differently, and quality can only be judged once the wines are made. A start in late August is early for Burgundy by historical standards, and the diary should be read as a first signal, not a verdict.

What a short crop means for a cellar is a general principle of the trade. When volumes fall, domaines tend to allocate to long-standing customers, and the bottles go first to those who have kept the relationship. The person buying for a house is rarely the person with the best claim on a scarce allocation, unless she has built one.
articles.why: A short vintage rewards the cellar manager who holds allocations and relationships, so reading a harvest report from the vineyard is part of the work of buying for a house.

articles.title: Personal assistants draw about 112 applications per search and butlers about 48, yet roughly four in five candidates are turned down, Morgan & Mallet's 2026 report shows
articles.body:
Morgan & Mallet's Household Staff Industry Report 2026, updated in June, draws on more than 450,000 applications since 2016 across 70 countries and a network of more than 56,300 vetted professionals in over 100 roles. About four in five candidates assessed are turned down. The firm's reading is that the market suffers from a shortage of suitable candidates, not of candidates.

The applications per search show where the scarcity lies. Personal assistants attract about 112, chauffeurs about 106 and estate or house managers about 80, against about 48 for butlers, 46 for private chefs, 37 for nannies, 34 for housekeepers, 26 for governesses and 24 for domestic couples. The butler figure rests on more than 7,800 applications across 167 searches, from a network of 1,882 butlers of 38 nationalities, 90 per cent of them men. The estate and house manager network counts 2,314, around 80 per cent men, with about 17 years of experience on average.

The vetting is the part a candidate controls least and should expect most. It runs to a 90-minute structured interview before any presentation to a client, reference checks with former employers, employment verification going back five to seven years, and criminal background screening. The workforce it produces spans 124 nationalities and 91 languages, with an average age of 43. French nationals are the largest group, followed by Filipinos by a wide margin.

The figures are the firm's own records and are not independently verified, and the report itself sets aside demand growth by country because it tracks the agency's expansion rather than the market's. Within those limits, one detail stands out. Domestic couples show the longest tenure, at 4.2 years, and butlers the shortest listed, at 2.6.
articles.why: The funnel described here is the one a candidate will face in practice, a long interview and five to seven years of history that can be checked end to end, so the preparation that matters is a record that stands up to verification.
articles.src: Morgan & Mallet Household Staff Industry Report 2026

briefs.t: The art market grew 4 per cent in 2025 to USD 59.6 billion
briefs.b: The Art Basel and UBS report, published on 12 March, counts dealer sales of USD 34.8 billion and public auction sales of USD 20.7 billion, up 9 per cent. Auction sales above USD 10 million rose 30 per cent, while online sales fell 11 per cent to USD 9.2 billion. The United States holds 44 per cent of the market, the United Kingdom 18 per cent, China 14 per cent and France 8 per cent.
briefs.src: The Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report 2026

briefs.t: Only about a third of family offices have a clear succession plan
briefs.b: UBS's Global Family Office Report 2026, published on 28 May, surveyed 307 offices with an average net worth of USD 2.7 billion. Some 27 per cent are preparing the next generation in a structured way, and 65 per cent have invested across the AI value chain. Sixty per cent plan to adjust their strategic asset allocation within a year.
briefs.src: finews.com, UBS Global Family Office Report 2026

briefs.t: London sold 34 homes above GBP 15 million in six months, worth GBP 1.24 billion
briefs.b: Beauchamp Estates counts sales up 79 per cent in value on the first half of 2025, with an average price of GBP 36.5 million. American and Gulf buyers took 55 per cent of the deals, and two sales topped GBP 100 million, the largest at Providence House in Chelsea for GBP 275 million. The figures come from a single agency's survey.

lead.title: An estate manager earns up to GBP 220,000 in London and USD 425,000 in the United States, but the figures are not built the same way, Oplu's 2026 salary guide shows
lead.standfirst: The staffing agency's benchmark, updated on 9 October, sets out what private households pay across the UK, the US, Monaco and Switzerland, and how much of the number is really accommodation, bonus or tax.
lead.body:
Oplu, a household staffing agency, published its Private Staff Salary Guide 2026 in April and updated it on 9 October. For the estate manager, the role at the summit of a private household, it gives a UK range of GBP 110,000 to GBP 220,000 or more, a US range of USD 160,000 to USD 425,000 or more including accommodation and bonuses, and, for Monaco and the South of France, EUR 8,500 to EUR 16,000 net a month plus accommodation and bonuses. The width of each range is the first lesson: the title covers everything from a single country house to a multi-property portfolio.

Below the estate manager the guide sets out a ladder. In the UK a house manager of a single significant residence is quoted at GBP 75,000 to GBP 115,000, a butler at GBP 65,000 to GBP 105,000 and a head butler of a large principal residence at GBP 95,000 to GBP 150,000. A private chef earns GBP 65,000 to GBP 125,000, while a head chef in a principal household reaches GBP 110,000 to GBP 190,000 or more. A senior career nanny, Norland-trained and working for an ultra-high-net-worth family, is quoted at GBP 95,000 to GBP 140,000 or more. In the US, a butler in a principal residence is quoted at USD 110,000 to USD 190,000, a private chef at USD 130,000 to USD 270,000 or more and a private chauffeur at USD 85,000 to USD 140,000.

The Riviera figures need translating. Oplu notes that tax-adjusted gross figures in Monaco and the South of France are often 20 to 40 per cent higher than the net sums quoted, and estimates that a housekeeper paid EUR 5,000 net a month implies an employer cost of roughly EUR 85,000 to EUR 95,000 a year. In Switzerland, where the guide quotes monthly sums without saying whether they are gross or net, a housekeeper is placed at CHF 5,500 to CHF 8,500 and a butler or chef at CHF 7,500 to CHF 13,000.

The guide is candid about its limits. Oplu says it benchmarks against its own live placements rather than published data, UK figures are gross annual and full-time, and the US and Swiss figures do not state their basis. It gives no figures at all for Italy, Spain or the UAE. The ranges are best read as the asking prices of one agency's client list, a useful map rather than a census.
lead.why: A manager who builds a team, or negotiates her own package, has to compare like with like: the currency, whether the figure is gross or net, and whether accommodation and bonus sit inside the number.

articles.title: Manhattan buyers signed 55 contracts on homes asking USD 4 million or more in two weeks, against a ten-year average of 47
articles.body:
Realtor.com, citing weekly data from Olshan Realty, reported on 12 October that 55 contracts were signed for Manhattan homes asking USD 4 million or more across the two weeks ending 4 and 11 October. The ten-year average for the same early-October stretch is 47. The latest week produced 25 contracts, and the week before it produced 30, the highest weekly total in nearly four months.

The figures describe signed contracts, not completed closings, so final prices may differ from asking prices and some deals may still fall through. They are best read as a measure of appetite at the top of the market rather than of money already changed hands. Corcoran's third-quarter report, as summarised by a New York real estate lender, recorded a 9 per cent year-on-year increase in completed Manhattan home sales.

For anyone who runs a principal's New York base, a busier autumn market matters in practical ways. A family buying or selling means surveyors, designers, movers, storage and temporary staff, and a household manager is often the person who coordinates access, security and discretion while the deal is live.
articles.why: A property transaction is a household project in disguise, and the manager who understands its rhythm can protect the family's privacy and routines while strangers walk through the house.
articles.src: ARCFE, citing Realtor.com and Olshan Realty

articles.title: A 35-metre expedition yacht will make its Fort Lauderdale show debut as the fair, which runs from 28 October to 1 November, spreads across six locations
articles.body:
The Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show runs from 28 October to 1 November and will host more than 1,300 boats across six show locations, among them Bahia Mar Yachting Center, Hall of Fame Marina, Las Olas Marina and Pier Sixty-Six Marina. Among the charter yachts joining the fleet is Stellamar, an expedition yacht of 114.1 feet, or 35 metres, built by Cantiere delle Marche in 2023.

The specification shows what a charter guest is actually buying. Stellamar has a steel hull and aluminium superstructure, cruises at 11 knots and has a stated range of 5,500 nautical miles at 9 knots. She sleeps up to 12 guests in five cabins, including a full-beam master suite with dressing room and study, and carries up to seven crew. Her toys include two SEABOBs, two Flyboards, four paddleboards and diving and fishing equipment, and she has two tenders, one of 11.89 metres. The listing gives no charter rate and refers readers to a broker.

The ratio of guests to crew is the figure worth noticing. Seven people sustain the experience of twelve, and the same arithmetic applies on land, where a house runs smoothly only when the work behind the scenes is invisible. Boat shows are where owners, captains, charter brokers and suppliers meet in a single week, which makes them one of the busiest weeks in the yachting year for anyone arranging travel for a principal.
articles.why: A show week concentrates yachts, brokers and decision-makers in one port, and the assistant who knows the dates, venues and logistics can plan a principal's visit well ahead of the crowds.

articles.title: The Yacht Rendezvous returns to Pier Sixty-Six on 6 and 7 November for its 37th year, with owners hosting children's club members on board
articles.body:
The Yacht Rendezvous, a fundraiser for the Boys & Girls Clubs of Broward County, returns to Pier Sixty-Six in Fort Lauderdale on 6 and 7 November, according to Megayacht News, which is a media sponsor of the event. It is the 37th annual edition. The first night is a yacht hop in which club members meet supporters and tour the yachts. The second is a gala at which young people share their stories.

The co-chairs, Carla Taylor, Jessica Busacca and Mike Busacca, told the publication that meeting the children is what brings owners back. Mr Busacca first attended as a guest about 20 years ago and became more involved after seeing the children's participation and the friendships among owners. The clubs offer young people skills development and a safe place to go, from computers and basketball to hot lunches, and club members also discuss college and career goals with attendees.

Philanthropy is a regular part of an owner's calendar, and events of this kind are often where a principal's giving becomes visible. The practical work falls to those around the family: invitations, seating, guest lists, tender transfers, crew briefings and the quiet management of who meets whom.
articles.why: Charitable evenings are part of how families are seen, and whoever coordinates the principal's diary needs to treat them as carefully as any business commitment.

briefs.t: Monaco employer costs run well above the net salary
briefs.b: Oplu estimates that a housekeeper on EUR 5,000 net a month in Monaco costs an employer roughly EUR 85,000 to EUR 95,000 a year once tax adjustments are included. The agency says gross figures are often 20 to 40 per cent higher than net.

briefs.t: Switzerland quotes butlers and chefs at CHF 7,500 to CHF 13,000 a month
briefs.b: The same guide puts Swiss housekeepers at CHF 5,500 to CHF 8,500 a month. It does not say whether the Swiss figures are gross or net.

briefs.t: A charter broker flags a payments disruption at OneFlight
briefs.b: Amalfi Jets, a charter broker, says OneFlight suffered a service disruption affecting payments and bookings in September, and that its current status is unconfirmed. The broker's October outlook covers Van Nuys, Teterboro, Miami-Opa-locka and Dallas Love Field.

lead.title: The world now counts more than 4,000 billionaires for the first time, Hurun finds, and China holds 1,110 of them
lead.standfirst: Hurun's Global Rich List 2026 records 4,020 people worth USD 10 billion or more, 578 more than a year ago, with combined wealth up 28 per cent.
lead.body:
The Hurun Global Rich List 2026 has crossed a threshold that would have seemed remote a decade ago: 4,020 individuals worth USD 10 billion or more, the first time the count has exceeded 4,000. That is an increase of 578 on the previous year, and the research house reports that the combined wealth of the group rose 28 per cent over the same period.

The geography of the list is shifting as much as its size. China leads with 1,110 billionaires, up 287, followed by the United States with 1,000 and India with 308. Elon Musk heads the ranking with USD 792 billion, an increase of 89 per cent, and holds the top position for the fifth time in six years. The figure differs from the one Forbes published for its own American list in September, which put Mr Musk at USD 908 billion: the two houses use different valuation dates and methods, a reminder that any single net worth figure is an estimate rather than a fact.

For the estate manager, a list of this kind is less a leaderboard than a map of future households. Each additional billionaire is a principal who may soon need a primary residence, a second and third address, a travel operation and a staff to run them. The new wealth in Asia in particular is creating families whose households are being built from scratch, often without the inherited habits of service that older European and American families take for granted. The professionals who can build those structures, and who can speak to principals in more than one cultural register, are the ones in shortest supply.
lead.why: Every new fortune is a household yet to be organised, and the people who will be asked to organise it are the ones who understand how private service is structured across cultures.
lead.src: The Standard (Hong Kong), on the Hurun Global Rich List 2026

articles.title: Fine wine has stopped falling, Liv-ex data suggests, and the auction rooms are selling nearly everything again
articles.body:
The fine wine market ended a difficult stretch in better shape than it began it. According to Decanter's June analysis of Liv-ex data, the major indices were broadly flat in the four months to 30 April 2026, with the Fine Wine 50, which tracks the Bordeaux first growths, the best performer at plus 0.7 per cent. Over the longer run the picture is mixed: the Liv-ex 100 rose 34.1 per cent in the ten years to the end of 2025, the Burgundy 100 rose nearly 106 per cent and the Italy 100 almost 61 per cent, yet the Liv-ex 100 remains 24.7 per cent below its 2022 peak, according to Knight Frank's Wealth Report 2026.

The auction rooms tell a livelier story than the indices. Sotheby's says it has sold 96 per cent of the lots it offered in 2026 so far, and Nick Pegna, its head of wine, dates the change to September of last year. A New York Bordeaux sale totalled USD 2.1 million, USD 800,000 above its high estimate, led by a magnum of Lafite Rothschild 1870 that sold for USD 200,000, four times its high estimate. In London, Christie's sold every lot of Andrew Lloyd Webber's cellar for GBP 517,910, and a three-bottle lot of Romanée-Conti Grand Cru 2005 made GBP 56,250 against a high estimate of GBP 45,000.

The structure of demand is changing too. Bordeaux accounted for close to 80 per cent of trade by value at Bordeaux Index in 2010, against nearly 40 per cent today, as collectors have moved towards Burgundy, Champagne and Italy. Among the most traded wines at Bordeaux Index were Château Latour 2016 and 2019, Sassicaia 2023 and Taittinger Comtes de Champagne 2006.
articles.why: A cellar is an asset, an inventory and a conversation piece at once, and the manager who can read where collectors are heading can advise on what to buy, hold and open.

articles.title: Frieze arrives in Regent's Park on 14 October and Art Basel Paris follows nine days later, and a principal's calendar fills accordingly
articles.body:
The autumn art fortnight is one of the busiest periods in the calendar of a collecting family. Frieze London and Frieze Masters run from 14 to 18 October in Regent's Park, according to Artnet News. Frieze London has 172 exhibitors, up from 166 in 2025, in its 23rd edition, while Frieze Masters has 140 participants, up from 120, in its 14th year. Several established galleries are not returning, among them Almine Rech, James Cohan, Sean Kelly and Kurimanzutto at Frieze London, and Pace at Frieze Masters, while Night Gallery and Pilar Corrias come back after a break.

Art Basel Paris follows from 23 to 25 October at the Grand Palais, its fifth edition, with more than 200 galleries from 41 countries and territories, a four-part structure of Galleries, Emergence, Premise and Magazine, and an off-site programme at nine venues across the city, including the Petit Palais. Ticket categories run from a reduced rate of EUR 30 to a permanent pass at EUR 130 for the three days, while First Choice and Preview cardholders receive free admission to partner museums such as the Palais de Tokyo and the Musée National Picasso.

For a household team the fairs are an exercise in logistics rather than taste. Previews and private viewings must be secured for the principal and for any adviser travelling with her, flights and hotels have to be fitted around two cities within ten days, and purchases may need to be insured, documented and shipped before the family has left town.
articles.why: Access to the right preview, at the right hour, with the right car waiting, is the kind of invisible arrangement that defines good private service during a fair week.

articles.title: Family offices pay executive assistants up to USD 190,000 as the role absorbs travel and household coordination, a CNBC survey of recruiters showed
articles.body:
A report published by CNBC in January 2025, still among the clearest published pictures of the market, found that executive assistants at family offices often earn base salaries above USD 140,000, with the top of the range reaching USD 190,000 at offices with billions in assets. The median base salary was USD 100,048 in a Botoff Consulting survey of 436 family offices and family investment firms, and offices with at least USD 2.5 billion under management paid a median about 35 per cent higher.

Annual bonuses typically run from 10 to 20 per cent of base, and the top 10 per cent of assistants earned USD 188,800 with a 20 per cent bonus. At the largest offices, all-in compensation for the top 10 per cent could reach USD 240,000. For comparison, the average senior executive assistant in the wider market earned USD 81,500, according to Robert Half.

The premium reflects what the job has become. Most offices want at least five years of related experience, and some ask for eight to ten. The work goes well beyond correspondence and expense reports to organising family travel and coordinating household staff at multiple residences, and assistants often travel with principals, sometimes monthly. One recruiter estimated that at least 10 per cent of the work may be personal-assistant duties. The pool of candidates with both discretion and polish is small, and family offices are competing for them with Wall Street.
articles.why: The role sits exactly where the household meets the office, which is why those who can run both a diary and a staff of several properties are paid well above the standard administrative scale.

briefs.t: Forbes puts Musk at USD 908 billion
briefs.b: The 2026 Forbes 400 of richest Americans, published in September, ranks Elon Musk first at USD 908 billion, ahead of Jeff Bezos at USD 378 billion and Larry Page at USD 278 billion. Mr Musk has led the list for five years in a row.

This year's Frieze Masters is themed Queering Modernism, with David Zwirner and Victoria Miro presenting work by Alice Neel in response. Frieze London adds a new section, The Code Universe, curated by Carol Yinghua Lu.

briefs.t: Family offices struggle to keep staff
briefs.b: An AlTi Tiedemann Global and Campden Wealth study of 98 family offices found that 70 per cent have difficulty recruiting talent and 65 per cent worry about retaining staff. The study, published in May 2024, put average chief investment officer pay at USD 821,000 at offices above USD 1 billion.

lead.title: Presence is replacing permanent residence, Knight Frank finds, as 129 people a day cross the USD 30 million line and London becomes a city to dip in and out of
lead.standfirst: Knight Frank's reading of the prime property market describes owners who hold many addresses and live fully in none, with direct consequences for the people who run them.
lead.body:
Global luxury residential prices rose 3.2 per cent in 2025, Knight Frank reports in its analysis of the Wealth Report 2026, extending a run that began in early 2023 and that has outpaced mainstream house prices. Of the 100 markets tracked by its Prime International Residential Index, 73 recorded gains. Behind the headline lies a more interesting shift in behaviour. Knight Frank's Pritchard puts it plainly: "presence is rapidly replacing permanent residence" among the most mobile buyers.

The divergence between cities shows what that means in practice. London prime values fell 4.7 per cent, yet super-prime rents there have risen 53 per cent over five years, and close to half of prime central London purchases are made without a mortgage. Knight Frank calls the capital the ultimate "dip-in, dip-out" city: a place families use for a season, a school term or a set of meetings, and rent or hold lightly. Paris rose 1.3 per cent. In Italy a EUR 300,000 flat-tax regime has produced deep shortages in Milan and is pushing buyers towards Rome and Lake Como. In New York prices rose 0.8 per cent but turnkey stock is scarce, and the Upper East Side is recording record transaction speeds. Miami absorbed about USD 3 billion of super-prime sales, with South Beach ultra-prime above USD 5,000 per square foot.

Asia tells a similar story with different numbers. The region averaged 3.6 per cent growth. Singapore rose 7.9 per cent and climbed from fifth to fourth on the index, despite a 60 per cent Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty that constrains volumes. Hong Kong fell 2.1 per cent but still recorded 81 transactions of USD 10 million or more in the fourth quarter, second only to Dubai.

The demand beneath all this is growing quickly. Knight Frank expects about 129 people a day to cross the USD 30 million wealth threshold over the next five years. Many will buy, rent or borrow several homes at once, in different tax and legal systems, and expect each to be ready on the day they arrive.
lead.why: A family with five addresses and no fixed home needs a house manager who can run continuity: staff, stock, security and paperwork that follow the principal from city to city. The estate is no longer one building but a network, and the person who keeps it coherent is the product.

articles.title: The world's ultra-wealthy population grew 14.4 per cent in 2025 to a record 556,850, Altrata finds, and will near 750,000 by 2030
articles.body:
Altrata's World Ultra Wealth Report 2026, published in June, counts 556,850 people with a net worth above USD 30 million, the strongest annual expansion since 2017 at 14.4 per cent. In two years the group has grown by almost 30 per cent, adding more than 120,000 people. Together they hold USD 63.8 trillion, more than twice the annual output of the United States, of which about USD 26 trillion is investable.

The geography is changing. North America adds the largest absolute number, about 77,000 more by 2030, taking it above 300,000 people, and roughly four in five of its ultra-wealthy are self-made. Asia grew 15.8 per cent in 2025 and has the strongest forecast growth of the three major regions, led by India, China, the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia. Altrata projects a global population of 746,570 and combined wealth of USD 85 trillion by 2030.

Two details matter for anyone who will serve these families. Women make up 12 per cent of the group today and Altrata expects 19 per cent by 2040. And purely inherited wealth accounts for only 6 per cent of the total, which means most of the households now entering the market built their fortunes recently and are assembling their first serious domestic organisation, rather than inheriting one.
articles.why: New money without a household tradition hires on trust and learns on the job. The manager who can explain how a well-run house operates, and set it up without condescension, is worth far more to such a principal than one who only follows inherited routine.

articles.title: North American business aviation rose 0.9 per cent in September, beating a forecast decline, as large-cabin fractional flying jumped 13.9 per cent
articles.body:
Argus International reported on 8 October that North American business aviation activity rose 0.9 per cent in September. The result defied expectations: the same analyst had projected, in its August review, a 0.1 per cent decline that would have been the first negative year-on-year month of 2026. The large-cabin fractional segment led, up 13.9 per cent.

The August figures show where the growth comes from. Overall activity rose only 0.3 per cent, well below a 3.5 per cent forecast, yet fractional flying was up 7.9 per cent, with large-cabin fractional up 14.9 per cent. Charter (Part 135) was flat at plus 0.1 per cent, while owner-operated flying under Part 91 fell 2.9 per cent, with midsize and large-cabin aircraft down more than 13 per cent. Argus analyst Travis Kuhn called August a seasonal transition month and said the market remained healthy.

The pattern is consistent: families are still flying, but fewer of them are flying aircraft they own and operate. Shares, cards and managed programmes are absorbing the demand, and with them the logistics of scheduling, catering, ground handling and crew coordination move from a flight department to a service contract.
articles.why: A concierge increasingly books capacity rather than directing a tail number. Knowing how fractional, card and charter products differ, and what each demands in notice, catering and customs planning, is now a core travel skill.

articles.title: Average tenure in private service has fallen from about 20 years to about three, and a butler now lasts 2.6 years, Morgan & Mallet reports
articles.body:
The Morgan & Mallet Household Staff Industry Report 2026 draws on the agency's own placement data, which it cautions is self-reported rather than independent research. Its headline is a collapse in tenure: from about 20 years in the traditional model to roughly three today. By role, a butler averages 2.6 years, a chauffeur 3.8 years and a housekeeper 4.0 years. The domestic couple, historically the anchor of a house, lasts longest at 4.2 years.

Pay explains part of the churn. Private chefs are placed at up to USD 300,000 in the United States, estate managers up to USD 250,000, butlers and nannies between USD 90,000 and USD 180,000, housekeepers USD 80,000 to USD 160,000 and chauffeurs USD 80,000 to USD 130,000. The United States and Switzerland together account for nearly nine in ten of the highest-paying roles placed. Estate managers draw about 80 applications per search and bring about 17 years of experience on average, making them the third most contested role; personal assistants attract about 112 per search.

The hardest posts to fill are not the best paid. Domestic couples draw about 24 applications per search, and 21 per cent of French clients report being unable to fill the role. In France, the net monthly cost of a couple has roughly doubled in a decade. Retention can be built: 91 per cent of New York private chef placements complete their full annual contract.
articles.why: If a three-year stay is now normal, the manager's real task is continuity: written household standards, handover files and a bench of trusted people, so that the house does not reset each time someone leaves.

briefs.t: A flat tax is draining Milan
briefs.b: Italy's EUR 300,000 flat-tax regime for new residents has created deep supply shortages in Milan and is pushing buyers towards Rome and Lake Como, Knight Frank reports. Families relocating on that scheme tend to need a house set up quickly, from staff to security.

briefs.t: Women are 12 per cent of the ultra-wealthy
briefs.b: Altrata counts women as 12 per cent of the world's ultra-high-net-worth population and expects 19 per cent by 2040. Principals are changing, and so are their expectations of household and family-office service.

Owner-operated flying fell 2.9 per cent in August in North America while fractional rose 7.9 per cent, Argus data reported by Private Jet Card Comparisons show. Midsize and large-cabin Part 91 flights were each down more than 13 per cent.
