lead.title: Monaco Yacht Show closes with 79 debuts and a brokerage fleet asking about USD 2.5 billion, as two yachts over 100 metres share the quay
lead.standfirst: The 35th edition, held from 23 to 26 September in Port Hercule, brought 117 superyachts and more than 560 exhibitors, and the youngest fleet the show has tracked.
lead.body: The Monaco Yacht Show closed on 26 September with a fleet that was larger, newer and more expensive than last year's. YachtBuyer, which tracks the event, counted 117 superyachts in the water against 116 in each of the two previous years, with a combined length of 5.58 kilometres and an average of 47.66 metres. The average age fell to 6.47 years from 7.28 in 2025, and 79 of the yachts were making a show debut. Forty-six had been delivered in 2026 alone. The headline pair were both owned by the game developer Gabe Newell, who acquired the Dutch yard Oceanco in 2025: the 111 metre Leviathan, delivered in November 2025 and making her first show appearance, and the rebuilt 93 metre Draak, a former charter yacht, berthed alongside. Among charter yachts the most discussed was the 102.4 metre Lürssen Nixie, delivered in June 2026, with a 270 square metre beach club and a Caribbean season ahead. Other debuts included the 80 metre Pangea, the first Amels 80 to be shown, the 72 metre Sanlorenzo Silver Fox, the yard's new flagship, and the 67.55 metre CRN Amor à Vida, the builder's first hybrid-propulsion superyacht. The commercial side was just as striking. Seventy yachts were offered for sale, up from 69 in 2025 and 65 in 2024, with total asking prices of about USD 2.5 billion and an average of USD 35.2 million. The three most expensive listings together asked EUR 415 million: the 72 metre Feadship Vanish at EUR 148 million, the 76.5 metre Feadship Boardwalk V at EUR 135 million and the 74 metre Amels Synthesis, freshly refitted, at EUR 132 million. The 75 metre Blohm+Voss Zeus, at EUR 77 million, returned to the brokerage market for the first time in almost a decade. The show itself is changing shape. A new Designer Gallery replaced the former Yacht Design and Innovation Hub, an Adventure Area gathered around 70 tenders, water toys and cars on a third quay, and a Blue Wake environmental programme counted 60 validated exhibitors. The organisers have confirmed that the 36th edition will run from 22 to 25 September 2027.
lead.why: For the person running a yacht programme or advising the family that owns one, Monaco is where charter availability, refit schedules and brokerage prices are read in a single week, and a younger fleet with more hybrid propulsion changes what the captain and the shore team need to know.

articles.title: Household staff pay is closing in on senior corporate salaries, with confidentiality adding 15 to 20 per cent, Morgan & Mallet's Beyond the Butler report finds
articles.body:
The family staffing agency Morgan & Mallet summarises the state of its market in six words in its Beyond the Butler 2025/26 report: demand is up and supply is down. Pay for the senior roles is now approaching that of senior corporate positions. In the United States, which pays the most for 60 per cent of all household roles, private chefs can reach USD 300,000, chiefs of staff USD 300,000, estate managers USD 250,000 and executive assistants USD 250,000. In the United Arab Emirates, compensation is expected to reach USD 120,000 to USD 140,000 as demand grows.

The report ties the pressure to how families now live. They are buying property in more countries, partly because of geopolitical uncertainty and looser monetary policy, and the end of non-dom status has pushed many families out of Britain towards Florida, Dubai and Switzerland. Estate managers account for 10 per cent of all requests in the United States, and the average tenure of a placement is about three years. In Britain, Brexit has made it harder for European citizens to work in households, which has pushed salaries up.

Privacy is priced explicitly. Confidentiality can raise pay by 15 to 20 per cent, and in Los Angeles 77 per cent of personal assistant roles require a non-disclosure agreement. Some households ban social media altogether and ask staff to hand over their phones on arrival. Technology is the other new requirement: in San Francisco, 83 per cent of positions recruited in the past year required comfort with integrated home systems, and staff typically need 8 to 12 weeks to adapt to a new household's set-up.

Nannies show the reverse pattern. Britain has the highest demand, at nearly a quarter of all placements, and worldwide nanny placements have a 96 per cent success rate, with candidates typically bringing six years of experience and first-aid training. Governesses are rare but in demand in Dubai and Saudi Arabia, and domestic couples remain among the most requested roles in Europe and the United States, at 21 per cent of top requests in France.
articles.why: The report sets out what a candidate is paid for: discretion, a command of home technology and the ability to run several properties, not formal credentials alone.

articles.title: Ninety-one heirs inherited a record USD 297.8 billion in a year, UBS finds, and USD 6.9 trillion will change hands by 2040
articles.body:
UBS's Billionaire Ambitions report, published on 4 December 2025, counted nearly 3,000 billionaires, up 8.8 per cent from 2,682, with total wealth at a record USD 15.8 trillion. Self-made billionaires added USD 386.5 billion, the second-highest annual increase in the report's history, and 196 new self-made names joined the list.

The transfer of wealth is the part of the report that matters most to household and family office staff. Ninety-one heirs inherited USD 297.8 billion, 36 per cent more than a year earlier. Multi-generational billionaires rose to about 860 from 805, controlling USD 4.7 trillion against USD 4.2 trillion. By 2040, roughly USD 6.9 trillion is expected to pass between generations, with at least USD 5.9 trillion going to children.

The survey, the eleventh edition, ran from 10 July to 25 September 2025. It found North America the top investment destination, named by 63 per cent of respondents, followed by Western Europe at 40 per cent and Greater China at 34 per cent.
articles.why: A change of generation often means a change of households, advisers and expectations, and whoever serves the family through a succession is working with new decision makers who may live very differently.

articles.title: Impressionist art rose 13.6 per cent in 2025 while whisky fell 10.9 per cent, as Knight Frank's luxury index slipped 0.4 per cent
articles.body: Knight Frank's Wealth Report, published on 23 April 2026, gives a clear picture of what collectors held and what they sold. Its Luxury Investment Index fell 0.4 per cent over 2025, but the categories moved in opposite directions. Impressionist art rose 13.6 per cent and watches rose 5.1 per cent, while classic cars fell 3.7 per cent and whisky fell 10.9 per cent. The year also produced a record for a modern work at auction: Klimt's Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer sold for USD 236.4 million. The same report found that high net worth individuals and family offices deployed USD 464 billion into commercial real estate in 2025, against USD 347 billion from institutional investors.
articles.why: A household that holds art, watches, cars and a cellar needs someone who knows which of those markets is rising, because insurance values, storage and the timing of any sale all follow the cycle.
articles.src: Family Wealth Report, citing Knight Frank

briefs.b: The Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show runs from 28 October to 1 November across seven venues, with superyachts over 100 feet moored at the 17th Street Yacht Basin. Serious buyers are advised to arrange access through brokers or exhibitors in advance.
Baglietto showed the T60 in Monaco, a 60 metre yacht of about 1,100 GT and the largest the yard has built, alongside the 50 metre FAST50 with a 30-knot top speed. Both were world premieres.
An AI robot on the Oceanco deck waved to visitors and drew wide attention on social media, and more than 560 brands exhibited in total. The 2027 show is set for 22 to 25 September.

lead.title: Dubai's family-office boom has outlived a war, but the families now keep a second address, UBP and Gulf Business report
lead.standfirst: The Dubai International Financial Centre counted 1,289 family-related entities in 2025, up 61 per cent in a year, yet the families arriving there are increasingly planning for a world in which the Gulf is one home among several.
lead.body:
The numbers behind Dubai's rise as a base for private wealth are large. According to an interview with Ahmad Chahidi, a senior wealth planner at UBP Middle East, first published by Gulf Business in August and republished by the bank in September, the Dubai International Financial Centre recorded 1,289 family-related entities in 2025, a rise of 61 per cent on the year before. Foundations, the vehicle of choice for families who want succession rules written down and enforceable, reached 1,115, up 66 per cent. Henley & Partners, for its part, put the net inflow of high-net-worth individuals into the United Arab Emirates at about 9,800 in 2025, the largest of any country.

Then came the war. On 28 February 2026 the United States and Israel opened an air campaign against Iran, and for the first time the Emirates were themselves targeted. IMI Daily's chronology records a reported strike near Jebel Ali port on 1 March, a drone hit on a tower at Dubai Creek Harbour on 12 March, and a brief closure of Dubai International Airport on 16 March. A ceasefire took hold on 8 April, though both sides have since been accused of violating it, and refinery fires at Fujairah in early May showed the region had not settled. The same commentary notes that enquiries from UAE-based individuals to one residence-by-investment adviser tripled between March and May compared with the previous three months.

The response of the wealthy has been less a flight than a hedge. UBP describes legal reforms that have strengthened the rules on wills, succession and cross-border enforceability, and foundation regimes are now available through the DIFC, the Abu Dhabi Global Market and Ras Al Khaimah. The bank also points to a transfer of nearly USD 2 trillion in wealth to the next generation across the Gulf Cooperation Council over the coming decade, which is what keeps families building structures there. Henley's own research adds the counterweight: enquiries from UAE-based individuals about alternative residence or citizenship rose 41 per cent between the last quarter of 2025 and the first of 2026. The pattern is one of families staying in Dubai while quietly acquiring a second base in Singapore, Switzerland, Italy, Greece or Monaco.

For a household that moves with its principals, this is a practical matter long before it is a financial one. A family with a Dubai residence and a newly opened second home in Geneva or Milan needs a manager who can stand up a household quickly, hire and vet local staff under two sets of employment law, and keep the principals' routines intact across both. It also needs continuity plans: where the children's schooling goes, how the household records travel, and who holds the keys when the family is elsewhere.
lead.why: When a family adds a second base, the household manager is the person who builds it, staffs it and keeps two homes running as one; the Gulf's recent shocks have turned that from a luxury into a standing expectation.
lead.src: UBP, interview first published by Gulf Business

articles.title: Lürssen delivers a record six superyachts in a single year, and more than a third of the world's 100 largest yachts now carry its name
articles.body:
The German yard Lürssen has handed over six custom yachts in 2026, which it describes as a record year. They are Odisea, Deep Blue, Boardwalk, O3, Nausicaä and Nixie, and they range from 75 to 140 metres in length. Marine Industry News reports that Lürssen now has more than 30 yachts above 100 metres in operation, and that by the yard's own count over a third of the world's 100 largest yachts were built by it.

The detail of the deliveries shows where owners are spending. Nixie, at 102.4 metres, was shown publicly at the Monaco Yacht Show and combines diesel-electric propulsion with energy storage, a 270 square metre beach club and a six metre wide aft pool. Another 2026 delivery has a battery installation that allows overnight operation without running generators, and a further yacht pairs diesel-electric propulsion with electric motor stabilisers. O3 is an expedition yacht built for long-range cruising, Nausicaä was designed by Marc Newson with a continuous glass ribbon around the guest deck, and Boardwalk is Lürssen's first yacht with a sliding hatch integrated into a retractable stairwell.

Lürssen says each project takes about four years and hundreds of thousands of manufacturing hours, and its sales director, Michael Breman, says the order book is strong and that no two Lürssens should ever be alike. That last point matters to the people who run them. Every large yacht is effectively a prototype, with systems, crew arrangements and guest spaces that differ from the last, and the first season after delivery is when the owner's household and the yacht's captain learn how the two worlds fit together.
articles.why: Quiet overnight running, beach clubs and glass decks change what a yacht asks of the shore team: provisioning, guest logistics and noise-sensitive schedules are now part of the family's wider household to plan.

articles.title: Empty-leg flights can cut a private charter bill by 25 to 75 per cent, but the discount comes with a cancellation risk, Spear's reports
articles.body:
An empty leg is the repositioning flight a private jet makes without passengers to reach its next charter. Spear's, citing the charter platform SkyAccess, reports that passengers who take these flights typically pay 25 to 75 per cent less than the standard price. London to Paris is the most popular international route, and London, Paris, Geneva and Nice were among the most frequent empty-leg destinations over the past year, a ranking that excludes the United States.

The seasonal pattern is predictable. Summer demand clusters around the south of France, Spain and Portugal's Algarve, and in winter the airports at Chambery and Sion fill with skiers. SkyAccess drew on twelve months of repositioning legs and currently listed future flights, and a route qualified only if it saw activity in at least three separate months.

The warning in the piece is the useful part. An empty leg depends entirely on the booking that creates it, so if the primary charter changes or is cancelled, the empty leg can vanish. Matt Feldon of the broker Smart Aviation says availability depends on how flexible the client can be with their schedule, that last-minute cancellations are not uncommon, and that he saw it happen three or four times this year with his own clients. His firm therefore tries to arrange few of them.
articles.why: A concierge is judged on the plan B: an empty leg may save a principal money, but it should only ever be offered with a confirmed alternative standing by.

articles.title: Singapore tops Henley's ranking of countries competing for wealthy residents, while Britain, France and Germany slip
articles.body:
Henley & Partners' Private Wealth Migration Report 2026, summarised by Wealth Professional in June, scores countries on how well they compete for mobile wealth. Singapore leads with 79.5, followed by New Zealand at 75.8, the Cayman Islands at 74.3, Cyprus at 73.5 and the Netherlands at 72.8. Portugal, Italy and Bermuda follow, and a strong second group at between 70.0 and 71.8 includes Uruguay, Hong Kong, Switzerland, Greece and Monaco. The United Arab Emirates scores 85.3, among the highest in the framework.

The countries under pressure are Germany at 69.7, Norway at 69.0, the United Kingdom at 68.3, South Korea at 66.2 and France at 65.7. Henley links the decline to tax changes, budget instability and shifting policy. The United States scores 62.3 despite being the largest private wealth market in the world, and applications to Henley from American nationals doubled in 2025 compared with 2024 and remained elevated into 2026. Only 7 per cent of those came from Americans already living abroad.

The firm received applications from 86 nationalities under 47 investment migration schemes in the first five months of 2026, and more than 28 per cent of applicants already lived outside their home country. Chief executive Juerg Steffen said governments could once treat their wealthiest residents as a relatively fixed asset, and can no longer do so.
articles.why: Where a family decides to live determines where its staff are hired, which employment law applies and which languages the household needs, so the league table is a map of where private service jobs will open.

briefs.t: Art Basel Paris returns to the Grand Palais with 211 exhibitors
briefs.b: The fair runs from 23 to 25 October, with preview days on 21 and 22 October, and brings 211 exhibitors from 41 countries and territories, nearly 30 of them new. It is the first edition under the direction of Karim Crippa.

briefs.t: Italy raises its flat tax for new residents to EUR 300,000
briefs.b: For those becoming tax resident from 1 January 2026, the annual charge on foreign income has risen to EUR 300,000, according to IMI Daily's review of destinations for Gulf-based families. Switzerland's lump-sum regime, still offered by 21 of 26 cantons, carries a federal minimum base of about CHF 435,000.

briefs.t: Dubai property trades hit AED 252 billion in a quarter
briefs.b: Transactions in the first quarter of 2026 rose 31 per cent on the year, IMI Daily reports, although Fitch has forecast a price correction of up to 15 per cent as about 250,000 new units complete through the year.

lead.title: Sotheby's will sell the Blaquier-Arrieta collection in New York on 18 November, twelve works led by a Van Gogh estimated at USD 180 million
lead.standfirst: The sale is expected to test both auction records set in 2022, for Van Gogh and for Cézanne, in a single evening.
lead.body: Sotheby's has announced that it will offer twelve works from the collection of the Argentine collectors Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and Carlos Pedro Blaquier in New York on 18 November, with a combined estimate of USD 450 million. The house describes the group as representing the development of painting in Paris from 1875 to 1905, and it is built around two pictures that each carry an estimate large enough to threaten a record. The first is Van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs of 1890, painted in his final weeks at Auvers-sur-Oise and estimated at USD 180 million. It was acquired from Wildenstein & Co. in New York in 1975. The artist's auction record stands at USD 118 million, set in 2022, so the estimate alone sits well above it. The second is Cézanne's Arlequin, painted between 1888 and 1890, a portrait of the artist's son in a harlequin costume, estimated at USD 120 million. It was once owned by Lord Rothschild and later bought from the Lefevre Gallery. The Cézanne record is USD 137.8 million, also set in 2022, which means the estimate sits just under it. Beneath the two leading lots, the supporting cast is substantial. Pissarro's Place du Théâtre-Français is estimated at USD 30 million to USD 40 million, Renoir's En Canot at USD 25 million to USD 35 million, and Degas's Avant la Course at USD 20 million to USD 30 million. Collections sold whole, with a continuous history of ownership by one household, tend to attract a different class of bidder from a mixed evening sale, because the provenance is part of what is being bought. For a family that holds work of this calibre, or that is advised to bid on it, the weeks before a sale such as this are a logistics project in themselves: viewings in several cities, condition reports, loan and shipping arrangements, insurance cover from the moment a work leaves a wall, and bidding by telephone through an adviser who must be reachable at the hour the lot comes up.
lead.why: A house manager or private assistant rarely buys the painting, but is often the person who arranges the viewing, the transit, the insurance cover and the quiet room from which the principal bids.

articles.title: Family offices are flying more, and almost all of them are letting more staff on board, an Airbus Corporate Jets study finds
articles.body:
A study published by Airbus Corporate Jets this month, carried out by the independent research firm Pureprofile among 73 senior executives of family offices that together manage USD 303 billion, finds that private aircraft have become the default way these organisations move. Some 96 per cent of respondents increased their use of private jets over the past two years, and private aircraft now account for 70 per cent of all aviation travel by the family offices surveyed. The fieldwork was carried out in May 2025, so the figures describe a market a little behind the present one, and the sample is small, but the direction is consistent.

The reasons given are practical rather than aspirational. Some 89 per cent of executives say a private flight saves two to three hours per trip, and 92 per cent report at least 25 per cent greater productivity on board. The most valued benefit is the freedom to work in flight, particularly on confidential matters. Two thirds of respondents make between 25 and 50 per cent of their trips to destinations without a direct commercial service, which is one reason family offices keep opening offices abroad: nearly 70 per cent have opened one in a new jurisdiction in the past five years, and 90 per cent of those cite family members living overseas.

The finding that bears most directly on a household is about who gets to fly. Some 92 per cent of respondents already allow more staff than before to use the family's aircraft, and 97 per cent expect that access to grow over the next three years. Looking ahead, 85 per cent anticipate raising their private aviation use by between 50 and 100 per cent in the next two years, with 43 per cent expecting a rise of 50 to 75 per cent in large jet use and 55 per cent expecting the same for medium-sized jets.

An aircraft that carries the principal, the family office team and a growing share of the household staff is no longer a private space in the old sense. It becomes a workplace with a manifest, a seating plan, a catering brief and a confidentiality policy.
articles.why: When staff routinely travel on the family's aircraft, the person planning the household's movements is also managing a manifest, ground handling at several airports and the discretion of everyone on board.

articles.title: The United States has created 41 per cent of the world's new USD 30 million households since 2021, and the house at the top of the market now comes with services attached, Knight Frank finds
articles.body:
Knight Frank's Residence Report 2026, published on 9 September by Liam Bailey, its global head of research, puts a number on the shift in where the world's wealthy people are being made. Some 41 per cent of all new individuals worth USD 30 million or more between 2021 and 2026 were created in the United States, and 35 per cent of the world's ultra high net worth population now lives there. The housing market at the top has followed.

In New York, the firm counts 341 super-prime sales in the year to the first quarter of 2026, up from 281 the year before, with attention concentrated on properties above USD 20 million. One new development in the West Village, 80 Clarkson, has generated more than USD 1 billion in sales, and a new sales record for the Upper East Side was set at 1122 Madison Avenue in February. In Los Angeles, super-prime sales are rising despite the city's Measure ULA transfer tax, and Beverly Hills, which sits outside the tax's jurisdiction, remains the focal point, with the Rosewood Residences Beverly Hills and the Aman-branded One Beverly Hills setting the benchmarks.

The report adds that Miami is the world's second-largest market for branded residences, with projects from Nobu, Mandarin Oriental and Four Seasons. Developers, Knight Frank notes, now compete through distinctive design, branded living and ever more elaborate amenities, with wellness facilities close to essential.

For the people who run these homes, the amenity floor matters as much as the address. A residence with a lap pool, a wellness suite and building-run services splits the work between the building's team and the family's own staff, and someone has to draw the line between the two.
articles.why: A branded or amenity-rich residence changes the job of the house manager, who must coordinate the building's services with the family's own staff and decide what is delegated and what stays private.

articles.title: A chief of staff to a private family now commands USD 200,000 to USD 370,000, and the gap above the estate manager is widening, Achieve Hospitality's 2026 guide shows
articles.body:
Achieve Hospitality's 2026 compensation guide for American domestic and household roles, drawn from what the agency describes as active placement data and market intelligence, sets out a clear ladder at the top of the profession. A chief of staff or director of properties is placed at between USD 200,000 and USD 370,000. An estate manager earns from USD 160,000 to USD 200,000, and a house manager from USD 120,000 to USD 160,000. A personal or executive assistant covers the widest range of all, from USD 80,000 to USD 200,000.

Below the management tier, the operational roles are more tightly bunched. A head butler is placed at from USD 100,000 to USD 120,000 and a butler from USD 90,000 to USD 100,000, with a head housekeeper at from USD 100,000 to USD 120,000 and a housekeeper at from USD 80,000 to USD 100,000. A private chef is listed at from USD 120,000 to USD 200,000, a chauffeur at from USD 90,000 to USD 120,000, and a close protection officer at from USD 90,000 to USD 150,000. In childcare, a rota nanny is listed at from USD 130,000 to USD 250,000 and a governess at from USD 150,000 to USD 250,000.

The agency does not disclose the size of its sample, so the figures should be read as the asking and placement levels of one firm, not as a statistical survey. They are useful for a different reason: they show where the title above estate manager has opened up. A chief of staff to a family usually oversees several properties, the household office and sometimes the interface with the family office, and the pay band reflects a job that is closer to general management than to housekeeping.

For a manager building a career, the ladder suggests a path. Experience in running a single residence leads to a multi-property estate role, and from there to a position that sits across the household, the staff and the family's advisers.
articles.why: The top of the ladder is where a house manager's skills in budgets, vendors and people become general management, and the salary bands show what the market pays for that step.

briefs.b: Frieze London and Frieze Masters run from 14 to 18 October at The Regent's Park, with Art Basel Paris following at the Grand Palais from 21 to 25 October. It is the first Art Basel Paris under its new director, Karim Crippa, with 211 exhibitors from 41 countries.

The largest yacht at last month's Monaco Yacht Show was Nixie, a 102.4 metre Lürssen delivered in 2026, among 43 yachts delivered this year that were shown in a single harbour. New commissions typically involve waits of 2028 or later, which is why a newly delivered yacht carries a premium.

briefs.t: Miami is the second branded market
briefs.b: Knight Frank ranks Miami as the world's second-largest market for branded residences, with Nobu Residences 619 Brickell, Mandarin Oriental at Brickell Key and Four Seasons Coconut Grove among the projects. Amenities such as wellness floors are now close to a requirement for developers competing at the top.

lead.title: America's private jet boom is built on tax breaks and public airports, Fortune finds, as global sales reach USD 40.3 billion
lead.standfirst: Private jets account for 7 per cent of flights handled by the Federal Aviation Administration but only 0.6 per cent of the taxes paid into the aviation fund.
lead.body:
Global private jet sales reached USD 40.3 billion in 2025, up nearly 24 per cent over five years and growing at an annual rate of about 4.7 per cent, according to figures cited in a Fortune investigation published on 1 October. The magazine estimates that around 256,000 people, 0.003 per cent of the world's population, make up the private jet class, holding some USD 31 trillion in wealth. The piece argues that the economics of that market rest heavily on public policy rather than on the owners alone.

The most important lever is tax. One Big Beautiful Bill restored 100 per cent bonus depreciation, allowing the full cost of an aircraft to be deducted in the year of purchase. Fortune calculates that a USD 40 million jet could cut a federal tax bill by as much as USD 14.8 million at the top 37 per cent rate. Eight American states offer full or near total sales tax exemptions on aircraft purchases, and Massachusetts alone is said to forgo USD 25.3 million a year through its exemption. Commercial passengers, by contrast, pay a 7.5 per cent federal tax on every ticket.

Public infrastructure completes the picture. Of USD 7.6 billion in federal Airport Infrastructure Grants, roughly USD 1.3 billion went to smaller airports that serve mainly private jets, with more than USD 1.1 billion directed at projects such as hangars and runway improvements. The National Business Aviation Association spent USD 3.4 million on lobbying across 2024 and 2025, and helped defeat a proposed 10 per cent luxury tax on aircraft priced above USD 500,000 in Washington state before it took effect. One chief executive quoted estimates that about half of private flights operate empty, a reminder of how much repositioning sits behind every departure.

For the households that fly, none of this changes the aircraft on the apron. For the people who run their travel, it is part of the background to scrutiny that may follow: public debate about private flying tends to resurface around fuel, emissions and tax, and families increasingly ask their teams to keep clean records of every sector, every empty leg and every guest.
lead.why: A concierge or house manager who arranges flights should understand how the family's aircraft is owned, taxed and used, because the paperwork behind each trip, from empty legs to guest manifests, is what the family will be asked to defend.

articles.title: North American family offices are turning optimistic, RBC and Campden Wealth find, in a survey of 155 offices with an average net worth of USD 2.25 billion
articles.body:
RBC and Campden Wealth published their 2026 North America Family Office Report on 2 October, drawing on 155 survey responses from single and multi family offices across the Americas. The families behind them range from USD 100 million to more than USD 10 billion in net worth, with an average operating net worth of about USD 2.25 billion. The central finding is a change of mood: families are described as raising their expectations and shifting from caution towards optimism.

The report frames its subjects as enterprising, holding what it calls a long term perspective and a position of patient capital. Its main themes are the great wealth transfer, the rapid creation of new wealth at the same time, the effect of technology on how offices operate, and the difficulty of balancing near term performance against succession planning across generations.

The full findings sit behind a subscription, and this edition therefore reports only what the publishers have made public. Even so, the direction is clear and consistent with the other large surveys of recent weeks: family offices are growing in confidence, growing in complexity and preparing for a handover between generations that will change who decides what.
articles.why: Optimistic families tend to spend, hire and build, and a generational handover usually reshapes household routines, so those who serve them should expect new principals with new expectations.
articles.src: IREI, citing RBC and Campden Wealth

articles.title: Hong Kong's autumn art auctions total HK$2 billion, up from HK$1.3 billion in spring, as Kusama works meet a cool reception
articles.body:
The autumn marquee sales in Hong Kong ran from 28 to 30 September and together reached about HK$2 billion, or USD 255.78 million, against HK$1.3 billion in the spring. Christie's made HK$956.5 million, up 17 per cent year on year, and reported a 30 per cent increase in young collectors among its new buyers. Sotheby's made HK$956 million, up 35 per cent on its March sales, with a 91 per cent sell through rate and five artist records.

The South China Morning Post described a disciplined market anchored by competitive depth for fresh to market works with strong provenance. Among the notable lots, Leonard Tsuguharu Foujita's 1932 painting Chatte et chaton was sold at Sotheby's on 28 September. Works by Yayoi Kusama, long a reliable draw in the region, received what the newspaper called a cool reception.

The lesson for a collector's household is that buyers are discriminating: provenance and freshness matter more than a famous name. That has practical consequences for those who look after collections, because documentation, condition reports and clean ownership histories are what support value when a work comes to market.
articles.why: A house manager who looks after a collection should keep provenance files, condition reports and insurance valuations in order, since in a selective market it is the paperwork that protects a work's value.

articles.title: Fine wine has not been this cheap since 2014, Liv-ex says, as trade rises by a third and mature Bordeaux draws buyers
articles.body:
The Liv-ex Fine Wine 1000 index has returned to its 2020 lows and to 2015 price levels, according to a September analysis in The Drinks Business. Prices are down roughly 40 per cent in real terms since 2022 and have halved relative to the FTSE index over the same period. Liv-ex chief James Miles said wine has not been cheaper since 2014, and added that prices bottomed out around this time last year, with supply and demand now at more normal levels. Trade is up by about a third compared with 2025.

The opportunity, analysts say, lies in mature Bordeaux. Early 2000s vintages are entering their drinking windows at 2015 prices, and Lafite 2000 is at its cheapest in 18 years. Wines from 2006 to 2010 show a healthy bid to offer ratio of 1.7, against 0.7 for wines from after 2020. Miles said it feels like a good time to start buying again, while cautioning against expecting a new bull run soon. Another analyst, Sophia Gilmour, noted that the longer term upward trendline has been broken.

Selectivity is the consistent advice: back vintage Bordeaux and top classified Burgundy, liquid and easy to trade, rather than emerging regions.
articles.why: Whoever manages a family's cellar needs to read the market as well as the cellar book: knowing which bottles are entering their drinking windows, and which are liquid, informs both what is served and what is bought.

briefs.t: Embraer delivers 41 jets in the quarter
briefs.b: Embraer delivered 41 executive jets in the third quarter of 2026, split nearly evenly between its light and midsize models. The manufacturer says it remains on track to meet its full year forecast.

briefs.t: Cannes opens the boat show season
briefs.b: The 49th Cannes Yachting Festival ran from 8 to 13 September with 700 boats, including 117 superyachts and a brokerage fleet of 62 yachts with combined asking prices of about USD 640 million. Azimut's Grande 44M, at 43.85 metres, led the debuts.

briefs.t: A staffing market set to double
briefs.b: Cora Partners notes that the global luxury household staffing market is forecast to nearly double over the next decade, growing at about 6.6 per cent a year. Estate managers, senior chefs and senior butlers face the most acute shortages.

lead.title: Carlyle has hired two senior executives to lead its family office business and set a target of USD 200 billion in new capital by 2028, after putting the addressable market for family offices at USD 5 trillion
lead.standfirst: The appointment of a former BlackRock relationship head and a family office veteran from Cercano Management shows how seriously the largest alternative asset managers now treat the family office as a client in its own right, rather than as an occasional co-investor.
lead.body:
Carlyle announced on 25 September that David Seeberan has joined as partner and global head of its family office group, moving from Cercano Management, the firm built around the fortune of Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen and dedicated to ultra wealthy individuals and family foundations. Seeberan is based in San Francisco and reports to Jeff Nedelman and Amal Alibhai. Alongside him, Victoria Matthews joins as managing director for Europe and Asia from BlackRock, where she managed the firm's relationships with family offices and endowments across the United Kingdom, and will work out of London.

The hires sit on top of a strategy Carlyle has been building since 2023, when it brought in Shane Clifford to lead its global wealth business, followed by Bill Ryan for retirement solutions. Carlyle now puts the addressable family office market at approximately USD 5 trillion and says it has raised roughly USD 50 billion from individuals and wealthy families since its founding. The firm is targeting more than USD 200 billion of new capital through 2028, with USD 90 billion of that earmarked for its credit business alone.

The logic is structural rather than opportunistic. As traditional institutional channels, pension funds and endowments among them, face their own constraints on new allocations to private markets, alternative asset managers are turning to affluent individuals and family offices as the next source of scale, building dedicated servicing teams, co-investment structures and reporting designed for a single family rather than a committee. It is a mirror image of the shift J.P. Morgan's own family office survey described this week: institutions professionalising to meet families, just as families have been professionalising to meet institutions.

For the household side of a family's affairs, the significance is less about the capital than about who now sits at the table. A family office that used to deal with a handful of relationship managers is increasingly served by dedicated global teams built specifically around its profile, complete with named leadership and public growth targets. Estate managers and chiefs of staff who coordinate with the family office on payroll, property and logistics are likely to find that side of the relationship becoming steadily more institutional, structured and metric driven.
lead.why: As the largest alternative asset managers build dedicated global teams to win family offices as clients rather than treat them as occasional co-investors, the professionalisation reaching the investment side of a family's affairs increasingly sets the tone the household side is expected to match.

articles.title: Rents for the ultra wealthy in prime central London have risen by more than two thirds this year, Beauchamp Estates finds, as buyers turn tenants amid Gulf instability and Britain's post non dom tax regime
articles.body:
Beauchamp Estates' Millionaires Letting in London survey, published on 22 September, puts the average annual rent paid by an ultra high net worth tenant in prime central London at around GBP 220,000. Rents for luxury houses and mansions have risen 67.15 per cent over the year, to GBP 4,177 a week, or GBP 217,204 annually, up from GBP 2,499 a week in 2025. Luxury apartments and penthouses have climbed a more modest but still sharp 15.12 per cent, to GBP 1,957 a week, from GBP 1,700 a week the year before.

The standout lettings this year include a Mayfair house on Mount Street at GBP 33,000 a week, or GBP 1.71 million annually, a Chelsea townhouse on Cheyne Walk at GBP 30,000 a week, and a One Hyde Park apartment in Knightsbridge at GBP 32,500 a week. Beauchamp attributes the surge to falling supply set against rising demand, with applications from Middle Eastern tenants up 30 per cent over the year, American applicants up 20 per cent and Chinese applicants up 5 per cent. The agency links the Gulf figure directly to regional instability, describing London as a safe haven for wealthy Middle Eastern families choosing to rent rather than commit to a purchase.

A companion survey from Spear's, updated on 26 September, helps explain why renting has become the more attractive option for some. More than 80 per cent of the property advisers it polled rated lifestyle and schooling, not tax treatment, as the strongest driver of a purchase, and while Dubai ranked highest for pure desirability, Valletta and London led for investment potential. Eighty one per cent of the same advisers backed introducing professional licensing for London's super prime brokers, on American lines, a sign the market they operate in has outgrown its old, informal structure.

A family renting rather than owning changes the terms on which household staff are engaged. Leases run on different timelines to freehold ownership, a change of landlord can unsettle staffing arrangements built around a specific property, and portable staff who move with the family rather than stay with the house become more valuable than ever. The rental surge in London is, in that sense, also a surge in demand for private staff who can be redeployed at short notice.
articles.why: As more ultra wealthy families choose to rent rather than buy in London, the household staff built around a single freehold address are giving way to staff hired to move with the family itself, a shift agencies and estate managers are only beginning to plan around.
articles.src: Beauchamp Estates, via Letting Agent Today

articles.title: Discretion outranks every formal qualification in the American household staffing market, Morgan and Mallet's analysis of 465 job briefs finds, appearing in three times as many requests as certifications
articles.body:
Morgan and Mallet International has published an analysis of 465 household job briefs handled across the United States between May 2022 and June 2026, covering more than 27 states. Discretion and confidentiality appear as a requirement in 61.3 per cent of all briefs, roughly three times more often than formal qualifications or certifications, which appear in 20.4 per cent. Prior experience in a private household is specified in 58.5 per cent of briefs, ahead of practical skills such as laundry and ironing at 43.2 per cent, cooking at 41.3 per cent and events and entertaining at 31.6 per cent.

Nanny roles account for the largest single share of briefs, at 19.1 per cent, followed by housekeepers at 16.8 per cent, then private chefs, house or estate managers and personal assistants. Geographically, three states account for 63.2 per cent of all briefs: California at 24.1 per cent, Florida at 23.0 per cent and New York at 16.1 per cent, with New York City, Miami and Los Angeles the leading cities. The single largest shift in the data is Braselton, Georgia, a small town whose share of national briefs rose 8.0 percentage points in 2025, the largest gain recorded anywhere in the country.

The employment terms behind those briefs are notably stable. Full time roles account for 95.2 per cent of specified positions and permanent roles for 93.3 per cent, while live in arrangements make up 39.6 per cent against 32.5 per cent live out and 28.0 per cent open to either. Minimum experience requirements run highest for butlers and formal service roles, at an average of 6.7 years, ahead of estate management at 6.3 years and childcare at 4.7 years. Among briefs specifying language ability, English appears in 75.8 per cent, French in 26.8 per cent and Spanish in 25.5 per cent, while specialist skills such as fine dining or Michelin experience, at 7.5 per cent, and yacht experience, at 5.2 per cent, remain comparatively rare.

The dataset puts a number, for the first time at this scale, on something recruiters and household staff themselves have long said informally: trust is the primary credential in private service, well ahead of technical training. For a student entering the profession, it is also a map of where demand actually concentrates, both by role and by geography, including in places, like Braselton, that would not appear on an obvious shortlist.
articles.why: Quantifying discretion as the single most requested trait in private service, ahead of any technical qualification, confirms what the craft has always taught informally and gives it, for the first time, a number a student can point to.

articles.title: Four Geneva watch auctions open within three days this November, led by Phillips' Geneva Watch Auction XXIV, after a spring and summer in which Hong Kong sale totals rose 90 per cent year on year
articles.body:
Geneva's autumn watch auctions fall across three days this year: Phillips holds The Geneva Watch Auction XXIV alongside Antiquorum's Important Modern and Vintage Timepieces sale on 7 and 8 November, Sotheby's holds its live Important Watches sale on 8 November, and Christie's closes the week with Rare Watches Including Watches for ELA on 9 November. Together the four houses make Geneva, once again, the fixed point of the collecting calendar even as the market's centre of gravity keeps shifting east.

The results feeding expectations into November were set earlier in the year. A first series Patek Philippe reference 2499 sold for approximately USD 10.2 million in Hong Kong in May, an F.P. Journe Tourbillon Souverain, nicknamed Chine 2010 38, made roughly USD 4.2 million the same month, and a unique white gold Cartier Cheich sold for close to USD 3.4 million in Hong Kong in September. Trade publication Haute Time describes Hong Kong's spring and summer auction totals as up 90 per cent year on year.

Three patterns are shaping the market ahead of the Geneva sales: rarity and one off commissions are commanding outsized premiums over even well known references, independent watchmakers continue to outperform pre sale expectations, and blue chip vintage Patek Philippe remains, in the trade's own words, the market's reserve currency. For the private service world, the pattern that matters most is logistical rather than aesthetic. Single pieces now regularly worth seven or eight figures move between family houses, bank vaults and travelling exhibitions, and it is increasingly a house manager or personal assistant, not the auction house, who arranges the insurance, the transport and the provenance paperwork that follows a watch from the sale room to the safe.
articles.why: As individual watches trade for eight figure sums and move constantly between houses, vaults and exhibitions, the private staff responsible for a family's collection are taking on logistics and provenance work that once belonged to the auction house alone.

briefs.b: UBS's Trends in Philanthropy 2026, drawn from its Global Family Office Report, finds 41 per cent of family offices worldwide now treat philanthropy as their primary channel for impact, ahead of operating businesses at 30 per cent and investment portfolios at 26 per cent. Of those managing giving in house, 68 per cent are building their own impact expertise rather than outsourcing it, and 27 per cent are folding philanthropy into the family's wider affairs rather than keeping it in a separate foundation.

briefs.t: The world's largest yacht, on schedule
briefs.b: REV Ocean, the 194.9 metre explorer vessel built at Norway's Vard for Kjell Inge Rokke, is expected for delivery in the fourth quarter of 2026 and will become the largest superyacht afloat at 19,235 gross tons. Among roughly ten major deliveries due before the year is out, Amels' 120 metre Project Tanzanite will become the largest Dutch built motor yacht in history, and Lurssen's 114.2 metre Project Cosmos will cruise up to 1,000 nautical miles on twin 500 kilowatt methanol fuel cells.

In Spear's 2026 survey of the advisers who serve super prime buyers, more than 80 per cent rated lifestyle and schooling as the strongest driver of a purchase, ahead of tax treatment. Dubai ranked highest for pure desirability, with 69 per cent of experts scoring it 4 or 5 out of 5, while Valletta and London led on investment potential. Eighty one per cent of the same experts backed introducing professional licensing for London's super prime brokers, along American lines.

lead.title: Running a family office with more than USD 1 billion under management now costs USD 6.6 million a year, J.P. Morgan's newest survey finds, and only 14 per cent have a written plan for replacing the people who run it
lead.standfirst: J.P. Morgan's 2026 Global Family Office Report puts a price, for the first time at this scale, on what it costs simply to keep a family office running, and finds succession planning for the office itself lagging far behind its own governance.
lead.body:
J.P. Morgan Private Bank's 2026 Global Family Office Report surveyed 333 single family offices, 197 based in the United States and 136 elsewhere, across 30 countries, together representing more than USD 500 billion in wealth. The average office in the sample runs USD 1.1 billion in assets under management for a family with an average net worth of USD 1.6 billion, and for the first time at this scale, J.P. Morgan has put a price on what it costs simply to keep that infrastructure running.

The costs rise sharply with size. An office overseeing USD 250 million or less spends around USD 875,000 a year to operate, rising to USD 1.7 million between USD 250 million and USD 500 million, USD 3.2 million between USD 501 million and USD 999 million, and USD 6.6 million once assets under management pass USD 1 billion. A family office, in other words, now has a cost curve as legible as a household's own payroll, and one that grows in the same direction.

Staffing that cost is where the report finds its widest gap. A chief executive or president sits atop 36 to 42 per cent of the offices surveyed, a chief financial officer in 20 to 32 per cent and a chief investment officer in 24 to 31 per cent, yet only 14 per cent of offices have a defined succession planning process for those roles, meaning 86 per cent would be improvising the day a senior executive left. Eighty two per cent maintain a formal investment committee and 80 per cent outsource at least part of investment management, evidence of real institutional structure sitting above a leadership bench nobody has actually planned to replace.

The family office has, in the space of a few reports like this one, become a staffed institution in its own right rather than a back office attached to the family, complete with a payroll, an org chart and now a documented cost of running it. For household staff and estate managers who sit alongside that office rather than inside it, the report is a reminder that the professional standard being set at the top of a family's operation, in governance, in succession, in cost discipline, is the same standard increasingly expected of the house itself.
lead.why: The family office is now costed and governed like any institution, and the succession gap showing up in its own leadership bench is the same gap recruiters have long described in the household, a reminder that professionalisation is arriving from both directions at once.

articles.title: More than a third of family offices report recruiting difficulty this year, a new compensation survey finds, and the chief financial officer has become the hardest role of all to fill
articles.body:
Botoff Consulting's 2026 Compensation and Talent Planning Survey, described by the law firm Katten as the most expansive proprietary dataset focused on family offices, finds recruiting has become the year's central operating problem rather than a peripheral one. More than a third of participating offices reported difficulty filling roles over the past year, a challenge that grows more acute, not less, at the largest and most complex offices.

The single hardest role to fill is the chief financial officer, particularly one who combines strategic planning with tax and estate planning expertise, and the survey finds a broader accounting talent shortage running across the sector. The underlying cause is less a shrinking pool of candidates than a widening one of employers: a surge in new family office formation, layered on top of the generational succession already reshaping who runs existing ones, has pushed demand for experienced talent well ahead of the supply able to meet it.

Compensation structure is moving to compete for that talent. Discretionary, one off bonuses are giving way to structured annual incentive plans built around individual performance, organisational results and investment performance metrics, and long term incentive plans, deferred compensation, co-investment and carried interest among them, are extending down into family office pay for the first time, a structure historically reserved for hedge funds and private equity firms.

For household staff and estate managers who often report through, or alongside, the family office, this is the vocabulary they are increasingly expected to share. Performance metrics, deferred compensation and carried interest used to belong only to the investment side of a family's operation, and are now part of how the whole household is being asked to think about pay.
articles.why: As family offices adopt structured, performance linked pay to compete for scarce financial talent, the household staffing market that estate managers and butlers enter is being pulled toward the same vocabulary and the same discipline.

articles.title: The global superyacht order book has fallen 4 per cent to 1,093 vessels, new industry data show, even as Italian yards tighten their grip on more than half of everything on order
articles.body:
Boat International's Superyacht Global Order Book 2026, presented locally by the Italian boating association Confindustria Nautica, counts 1,093 yachts on order worldwide, down 4 per cent from 1,138 a year earlier. Italy's own share of that order book rose two percentage points to 52 per cent, meaning 568 of the yachts currently under construction anywhere in the world are being built on an Italian slipway.

The decline in raw numbers sits alongside continued financial health among the yards themselves. Half of the shipyards surveyed reported turnover increases over the past year and a quarter reported stability, while roughly half kept their own order books at prior year levels and a quarter grew them, a pattern that reads less like a market in retreat than one consolidating around fewer, larger and more complex builds.

The scale behind those figures is considerable. Italy's wider nautical sector generated EUR 13 billion in added value in 2024 and employed 168,000 people, with headcount growing 5.6 per cent even as the number of yachts on order declined, a sign that much of the industry's value now sits in outfitting, systems and refit work rather than in hull count alone.

For the crew and shoreside teams a concierge eventually coordinates around a family's yacht, a smaller but more concentrated order book means a longer wait for a new build slot but a deeper, more specialised Italian supply chain, from carpentry to systems integration, to draw crew and after sales service from once she is delivered.
articles.why: A smaller but more concentrated order book, deepening in Italy specifically, is the same supply chain a concierge draws on for crew placement, refit scheduling and after sales service long after a yacht is delivered.
articles.src: SuperYacht24, citing Boat International and Confindustria Nautica

articles.title: Online interest in residency and citizenship by investment has risen more than eightfold in a decade, new research finds, as Malta's programme closes and Argentina prepares to open one
articles.body:
Analysis published in September by CEOWORLD magazine finds search interest in residency by investment and citizenship by investment programmes has risen more than eightfold over the past ten years, with more than 100 countries now operating some form of investment migration scheme.

Portugal remains the preferred destination for American and British applicants through its EUR 500,000 investment visa route, with Malta and Italy named as established alternatives. Malta's own decade old scheme, which generated EUR 1.4 billion over its lifetime, closed in 2025 following a European Union court ruling against it, removing one of Europe's longest running routes at the same moment that Greece and Panama are gaining attention, the latter through a USD 300,000 real estate route.

The market's next entrant may be its largest single economy yet. Commentary accompanying the research points to an expected citizenship by investment programme from Argentina before the end of the year, which would mark a materially larger economy entering a field so far dominated by small states and city economies.

Each of these programmes converts, on the ground, into a household opened or a household relocated, the estate manager's own paperwork mirroring the investor's, and Malta's closure is a reminder that the mobility a family buys can be legislated away almost as quickly as it was created.
articles.why: Every residency route opened or closed here is, in practice, a household being built or wound down elsewhere, work that lands on estate managers and staffing agencies long after the investment decision itself is made.

articles.title: A single 1980 Diego Giacometti console fetched close to USD 4.6 million in Paris last month, leading a run of autumn sales in which documented history, not rarity alone, decided the result
articles.body:
At Sotheby's Paris, a 1980 bronze console table by Diego Giacometti, titled Homage to Boecklin and sold as part of the Rochas Collection, achieved roughly USD 4.56 million, reinforcing how strongly the decorative arts market continues to reward single owner, well documented design furniture over comparable pieces without a clear history.

In New York, Christie's dispersed the complete 181 print Alan Medaugh collection of Hiroshige woodblocks for a combined USD 6.99 million. A single sheet, Plum Estate, Kameido, took USD 358,400 against an estimate of USD 60,000 to USD 100,000, a result the house's specialists attributed to the rarity of finding the set intact rather than to any single image.

Both results extend a pattern running through the month's design and Asian art sales more broadly, in which an unbroken, well kept chain of ownership is doing more to move a price than the object's rarity on its own.

For whoever manages a family's collection, the lesson across an entire season's results is consistent. A console or a print set with clean, complete paperwork is outperforming rarer or equally fine objects without it, which makes the private collection manager's own records as much a driver of value as the object in the vitrine.
articles.why: Across an entire season's results, documented provenance is doing more to move a price than rarity alone, which makes the private collection manager's own records part of what a family's holdings are actually worth.

briefs.b: Business jet flights rose 4 per cent worldwide in the first half of 2026 to 1.95 million departures, led by North America's 5 per cent growth and 72 per cent share of all flights. Fractional ownership was the most dynamic segment, up 11.5 per cent, with NetJets alone accounting for 13.6 per cent of global departures, while flying in the Middle East fell 17.8 per cent amid geopolitical tension.

Liv-ex's midyear data show the broad fine wine market barely moving, its flagship Liv-ex 100 index up just 0.4 per cent so far in 2026, while Italy's own index rose 1.5 per cent on the strength of Tuscan names such as Soldera Case Basse and Masseto, some vintages of which gained more than 20 per cent over the year. Bordeaux, by contrast, slipped 0.3 per cent over the same period.

New research from AlTi Tiedemann Global and Campden Wealth, surveying 126 family offices between February and May 2026, finds 48 per cent have now formally defined their wealth's purpose, up from 33 per cent a year earlier, most often to guide the next generation. Yet 71 per cent admit they have not yet fully engaged that next generation in the conversation.

A 1982 Rickenbacker 330 guitar played by Johnny Marr on Oasis's Definitely Maybe sold at Christie's London for roughly USD 474,500 against an estimate of USD 79,000 to USD 105,900, another instance this season of a well documented history moving a price several times past its estimate.

lead.title: Four in ten family offices have suffered a cyber attack in the past two years, a new survey finds, and the household staff who hold a family's calendar are increasingly where an attacker gets in
lead.standfirst: Ocorian's commissioned research finds 43 per cent of family offices breached within two years and a fifth with no defence plan at all, a gap that runs straight through the household staff who manage a principal's diary, travel and home network.
lead.body:
Ocorian, a corporate and fiduciary services firm, commissioned PureProfile to survey 200 family offices and family members representing USD 119.37 billion in managed or owned wealth, across the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Mauritius, South Africa, India, Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, the United States and several offshore centres. The results, published in June and reported by Family Wealth Report, found that 43 per cent of family offices globally had experienced a cyber attack within the past two years.

The gaps sit alongside genuine effort. Seventy five per cent of respondents said they had strengthened their defences over the same two years, yet nearly 20 per cent still have no defence plan of any kind, though 18 per cent of those say one is coming, and 22 per cent have no incident response plan to follow if an attack happens. Only 7 per cent had a plan in place more than two years ago, which suggests most of the field is still building its response after the fact rather than before it.

Outsourcing is where the trend is heading. Seventy two per cent of family offices expect to increase their cyber security outsourcing over the next three years, 41 per cent of those expecting a dramatic increase, and close to half already receive some third party support. More than one in ten described themselves as significantly challenged simply delivering the expertise internally, which is a striking admission from organisations built to manage far larger sums than most companies their size.

For whoever runs the household day to day, the practical exposure rarely looks like a headline breach. It looks like a calendar invite, a courier confirmation or a message that appears to come from the principal's own assistant, and the private staff who hold access to a family's diary, travel bookings and home network are, in practice, as much a part of the attack surface as any laptop in the family office itself. Training in basic cyber hygiene, verifying requests through a second channel and knowing what never gets confirmed by email are becoming as core to the role as any of the discretion a household has always been expected to keep.
lead.why: Cyber security in a private household is no longer a function the family office alone owns, it runs through every member of staff who touches a principal's calendar, travel or home network, which makes basic digital hygiene as much a part of the craft as discretion itself.

articles.title: Wealth is moving faster than governments can legislate for it, Henley and Partners' newest migration report finds, as tax changes reshape where the ultra wealthy call home within months rather than years
articles.body:
Henley and Partners' Private Wealth Migration Report 2026 describes a millionaire population that has become markedly more responsive to policy change. Decisions about where to base a family that once took years to shift, the report finds, can now move within months of a single tax announcement. The United Kingdom is the clearest case in point: the abolition of the non dom regime and the closure of the investor visa route have both been named as drivers of outflow, pushing wealthy residents to weigh a move that, a few years ago, most would not have considered.

The beneficiaries are concentrated. The United Arab Emirates remains, in the report's words, one of the world's leading centres for internationally mobile wealth, continuing to draw relocating families and their capital. Mediterranean destinations are also gaining ground, Italy foremost among them after its flat tax threshold for new resident income rose to EUR 300,000 from 1 January 2026, a change the report treats as a case study in how quickly a single fiscal decision now moves the wealthy population that a household staffing market ultimately serves.

For the household side of a relocation, the report's own language, decisions taking effect within months rather than years, is the operative detail. A family that moves its base, or simply adds a second or third one, needs staff, payroll structures, work permits and duty of care rebuilt on a timeline set by tax policy rather than by the usual pace of hiring, and estate managers and family offices increasingly report being asked to plan for a move well before the family itself has confirmed it.
articles.why: When wealth migration moves on a policy timeline measured in months, the household infrastructure behind it, staff, payroll, visas and duty of care, has to be able to move on the same timeline, which is now as much a test of an estate management team as of a family's tax adviser.

articles.title: Superyacht crew salaries are climbing across almost every rank in 2026, a new industry guide finds, as owners compete for the same small pool of experienced captains and chief stewardesses
articles.body:
YPI Crew's 2026 salary guide sets out pay by vessel size across the ranks that run a superyacht. A captain on a yacht under 30 metres now earns from EUR 5,000 to EUR 6,000 a month, rising through the brackets to from EUR 16,000 to EUR 23,000 on an 80 to 100 metre yacht, and a largely discretionary figure above 100 metres, typically from EUR 9,500 upward under equal rotation schedules. Chief stewardesses and heads of housekeeping range from EUR 7,000 to EUR 8,500 on a 40 to 50 metre yacht up to EUR 8,500 or more on anything over 100 metres, while head chefs range from EUR 4,500 to EUR 6,000 on the smallest yachts up to EUR 10,000 or more on the largest.

The guide does not point to a single dramatic shortage, but its own language describes what is functionally one: increased competition for experienced crew and rising expectations around work life balance, it says, are what is now driving salary and leave structures, with packages increasingly built around qualifications, certifications and onboard responsibility rather than tenure alone.

The pattern will be familiar to anyone following the onshore household staffing market in these pages: the same scarcity premium reshaping estate manager and butler pay ashore is now visible afloat, concentrated at the same senior, hardest to replace roles. Crew and household staffing agencies increasingly work across both markets, cross referring candidates between a yacht's deck and a family's shore based residence as owners try to build one coherent team rather than two separate ones.
articles.why: The scarcity premium reshaping household staffing onshore is now setting pay afloat too, and a concierge coordinating a family's yacht season increasingly needs to understand both markets as one.

articles.title: Monterey Car Week's 2026 auctions brought in USD 718.3 million, a rise of 66 per cent on last year, in a collector car market now sharply split between the exceptional and the merely rare
articles.body:
Across the week's main auction houses, and excluding a separate USD 40 million Ferrari Luce charity sale, Monterey Car Week's 2026 auctions totalled USD 718.3 million, up from USD 432.7 million in 2025 and from USD 471.2 million in 2022, the last comparable post pandemic peak. The top results were led by a Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe, sold by Gooding Christie's for USD 42.905 million, a record for an American built car, a McLaren F1 GTR at RM Sotheby's for USD 34.655 million, and a Ferrari F50 at Mecum for USD 14.575 million, a new public auction record for the model.

The results were not uniform. Broad Arrow's sell through rate reached 85 per cent, while other houses saw more mixed results, and several ambitious estimates across the week went unmet. Editors covering the sales described a market that has become sharply stratified: cars with strong specification, documented originality and a clean ownership history commanded serious competition, while rarity on its own no longer guaranteed a result.

For a family with a car collection, the practical reading is that provenance paperwork, build sheets, service history and an unbroken chain of ownership, is now as material to value as the object itself. That is a documentation burden that increasingly falls to a private collection manager or house archivist rather than to the owner personally, and a household that has let its own records lapse is, on this week's evidence, sitting on value it cannot yet prove.
articles.why: For whoever manages a family's collection, a week like this is a reminder that documentation, not rarity alone, is now what a strong result actually rewards.

articles.title: New York's ultra wealthy families are rebuilding childcare from the ground up in 2026, moving from a single nanny to full teams as senior salaries reach USD 200,000
articles.body:
Research from Eden Private Staff into how New York's ultra wealthy families are rethinking childcare finds senior nannies now earning from USD 120,000 to more than USD 180,000, and luxury household positions running from USD 150,000 to more than USD 200,000, against from USD 75,000 to USD 85,000 for entry level candidates and from USD 90,000 to USD 120,000 for mid level ones. Specific offers cited include USD 150,000 with a Manhattan apartment, health insurance and pension, and USD 180,000 with enhanced benefits attached. The city these families are hiring in is a large one: New York counts 384,500 high net worth individuals, 818 centi millionaires and 66 billionaires among its residents.

The structural shift matters more than any single salary figure. Families are moving away from a single nanny model toward professional childcare teams, increasingly built around a rota system of one or two weeks on and off, and toward combined nanny governess roles that fold newborn expertise, early years education, multi child experience, travel readiness and formal discretion protocols into one senior position coordinated with the rest of the household.

Formalisation is following the money. Healthcare, paid vacation, overtime structures and retirement contributions are now described as standard expectations rather than negotiated extras, part of the same professionalisation that agencies have reported across household staffing more broadly this year.
articles.why: Childcare is following the rest of the household into professionalised, team based structures, which is where a growing share of the profession's senior roles for graduates entering private service will sit.

articles.title: Dubai recorded 500 home sales above USD 10 million last year, Knight Frank's newest prime property index finds, as the Middle East overtakes every other region for luxury housing growth
articles.body:
Knight Frank's Prime International Residential Index for 2026 recorded global prime price growth of 3.2 per cent in 2025, down slightly from 3.6 per cent in 2024. Of the 100 markets it tracks, 73 rose in value and 24 fell. The Middle East led every region for performance, followed by Latin America and the Caribbean, with Asia Pacific and Europe close behind, while North America was the only region in negative territory overall, weighed down chiefly by weakness in Canada.

Dubai led the Middle East's performance with 500 home sales above USD 10 million in 2025, and Knight Frank names the United Arab Emirates the global leader in super prime residential performance, with Abu Dhabi now emerging as a destination for ultra high net worth buyers in its own right. Hong Kong recorded one of its strongest upticks in super prime sales at the end of 2025, Singapore continues to set price records despite constrained supply, and Aspen posted its third highest annual sales volume on record.

Europe shows the clearest sign of tax driven relocation within the same index. London is losing capital tied directly to the tax rule changes described elsewhere in this edition, while Milan and Madrid are capturing a share of that mobile capital as second home destinations for the families leaving.

Each of these markets is also, on the ground, a hiring market. A prime purchase in Dubai or Abu Dhabi typically arrives with a request to staff the property from scratch, while a departure from London usually means winding a household down rather than building one, and both jobs fall to the same estate management profession working from opposite ends of the same transaction.
articles.why: Every relocation on this index is, on the ground, a household being opened or closed, work that falls to estate managers and staffing agencies rather than to anything the index itself counts.

briefs.b: Frieze London and Frieze Masters return to Regent's Park from 14 to 18 October 2026 with close to 300 galleries between them, 172 at Frieze London and nearly 140 at Frieze Masters, drawn from 48 countries and regions, a slight increase on 2025's 282 galleries from 45 countries. New arrivals include London's Alice Amati and Galerina, Paris's Galerie Jocelyn Wolff and Kyiv's Voloshyn Gallery.

NetJets expects to take delivery of more than 80 factory new aircraft in 2026, expanding a fleet that already numbered 826 at the end of last year and flies roughly 1,440 flights a day. More than half of this year's expected deliveries were pre sold as of last autumn, evidence of how far ahead owners are now booking capacity at the top of the private aviation market.

briefs.t: A record CHF 75 million in Geneva
briefs.b: Phillips' Geneva Watch Auction XXIII totalled CHF 75 million, about USD 96 million, across 224 lots in May, the highest total in the series' history, with 43 world records set and 14 timepieces exceeding CHF 1 million. A Patek Philippe reference 2523 with a South America dial led the sale at CHF 7,961,000, followed by an F. P. Journe Chronometre a Resonance Souscription at CHF 4,875,500.

briefs.t: Nine per cent of billionaires plan to move
briefs.b: UBS's latest billionaire research puts global billionaire wealth at USD 15.8 trillion across nearly 3,000 individuals, with 9 per cent considering relocation, mostly to Switzerland, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates. Quality of life, geopolitical concern and tax efficiency, cited by 36, 36 and 35 per cent of respondents respectively, are named as the leading reasons to move.
